title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Group 1 Elements: Alkali Metals Physical & Periodic Invariants
content:
## 1. Group 1 Elements: Alkali Metals Physical & Periodic Invariants

### 1.1 Electronic Configurations & Atomic/Ionic Radii
* **General Electronic Configuration:** $[ \text{Noble Gas} ] ns^1$.
* The solitary valence $s$-electron is shielded effectively by inner electron shells, resulting in low effective nuclear charge ($Z_{\text{eff}}$), largest atomic and ionic radii in their respective periods, and minimal first ionization enthalpies ($IE_1$).
* **Radii Trend (Increases Down the Group):**
  $$\text{Atomic Radius: } \mathbf{\text{Li} < \text{Na} < \text{K} < \text{Rb} < \text{Cs}}$$
  $$\text{Ionic Radius: } \mathbf{\text{Li}^+ (76\text{ pm}) < \text{Na}^+ (102\text{ pm}) < \text{K}^+ (138\text{ pm}) < \text{Rb}^+ (152\text{ pm}) < \text{Cs}^+ (167\text{ pm})}$$


---


### 1.2 Density Trend & The Potassium Anomaly
Alkali metals are characterized by unusually low densities due to their large atomic volumes. They are light metals ($\text{Li}, \text{Na}, \text{K}$ are lighter than water):
* **Normal Expectation:** Density should increase down the group as atomic mass increases faster than atomic volume.
* **The High-Yield Inversion Anomaly:**
  $$\mathbf{\text{Density Order:}\quad \text{Li}\ (0.53) < \text{K}\ (0.86) < \text{Na}\ (0.97) < \text{Rb}\ (1.53) < \text{Cs}\ (1.90)\ \text{g/cm}^3}$$
* **Physical Origin:** Potassium ($\text{K}$) has an anomalous increase in atomic volume due to the presence of vacant, diffuse $3d$-subshell orbitals in the inner core, which expands the lattice volume disproportionately relative to its mass increase. Consequently, **potassium is lighter than sodium**.


---


### 1.3 Hydration Enthalpy, Hydrated Radii, & Ionic Mobility
Because hydration enthalpy is governed by electrostatic charge density:
$$\Delta H_{\text{hyd}} \propto \frac{z^2}{r}$$
* **Hydration Enthalpy Trend (Decreases Down Group):**
  $$\mathbf{\text{Li}^+\ (-506) \gg \text{Na}^+\ (-406) > \text{K}^+\ (-322) > \text{Rb}^+\ (-297) > \text{Cs}^+\ (-264)\ \text{kJ/mol}}$$
* **Hydrated Radii in Aqueous Solution:**
  Because $\text{Li}^+$ has the highest charge density, it binds the largest shell of water molecules:
  $$\mathbf{\text{Hydrated Radius:}\quad \text{Li}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{Na}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{K}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{Rb}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{Cs}^+_{\text{aq}}}$$
* **Ionic Mobility & Electrical Conductance in Water:**
  Larger hydrated spheres encounter higher frictional resistance moving through aqueous media:
  $$\mathbf{\text{Ionic Conductance / Mobility:}\quad \text{Cs}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{Rb}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{K}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{Na}^+_{\text{aq}} > \text{Li}^+_{\text{aq}}}$$
* **Hydrate Salt Formation:** $\text{Li}^+$ is the only alkali metal cation that forms hydrated crystalline salts (e.g., $\text{LiCl} \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$); salts of $\text{Na}^+, \text{K}^+, \text{Rb}^+, \text{Cs}^+$ do not form solid hydrates.


---


### 1.4 Visual Preservation: Periodic Invariants & Flame Photometry


![s-Block Periodic Trends, Density Inversion, and Flame Colors](/media/s_block_periodic_trends_density_and_flame_colors.webp)
*Description: Two-panel inorganic chemistry comparative graphic: (A) Physical trends and thermodynamic invariants of s-block elements detailing the potassium density anomaly ($\text{Li} < \text{K} < \text{Na} < \text{Rb} < \text{Cs}$), hydration enthalpy vs. hydrated radius inverse relationships, and the thermodynamic Born-Haber cycle explaining the extreme aqueous reducing power of lithium ($E^\circ = -3.05\text{ V}$); (B) Flame photometry spectra matrix displaying Bunsen flame emission colors, wavelengths, and electronic excitation physics for $\text{Li}$ (crimson red), $\text{Na}$ (golden yellow), $\text{K}$ (violet), $\text{Rb}$ (red violet), $\text{Cs}$ (sky blue), $\text{Ca}$ (brick red), $\text{Sr}$ (crimson red), $\text{Ba}$ (apple green), and explaining why $\text{Be}$ and $\text{Mg}$ produce no flame color.*


---


### 1.5 Flame Photometry & Photoelectric Applications
* **Flame Emission Mechanism:** In a non-luminous Bunsen flame, thermal energy excites the loosely bound outer $s$-electron to higher energy levels. When the excited electron cascades back to the ground state, it emits radiation in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum:
  * **Lithium ($\text{Li}$):** Crimson Red ($670.8\text{ nm}$)
  * **Sodium ($\text{Na}$):** Golden Yellow ($589.2\text{ nm}$, Sodium D-lines)
  * **Potassium ($\text{K}$):** Violet / Lilac ($766.5\text{ nm}$)
  * **Rubidium ($\text{Rb}$):** Red Violet ($780.0\text{ nm}$)
  * **Caesium ($\text{Cs}$):** Sky Blue ($455.5\text{ nm}$)
* **Photoelectric Utility:** Potassium and Caesium possess ultra-low ionization enthalpies and low work functions ($\phi$). Shining visible light ejects photoelectrons effortlessly, making $\text{Cs}$ and $\text{K}$ ideal for photoelectric cells and solar sensors.


---


### 1.6 Reducing Power Thermodynamics: The Lithium Super-Reducing Anomaly
* **Observation:** In the gas phase, reducing power tracks ionization energy: $\text{Cs} > \text{Rb} > \text{K} > \text{Na} > \text{Li}$. However, in aqueous solution, **Lithium is the most powerful reducing agent in the entire Periodic Table** ($E^\circ = -3.05\text{ V}$):
  $$\mathbf{\text{Aqueous Reducing Power:}\quad \text{Li} > \text{Cs} > \text{Rb} > \text{K} > \text{Na}}$$
* **Thermodynamic Analysis via Born-Haber Cycle:**
  $$\text{M}(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta H_{\text{sub}}} \text{M}(g) \xrightarrow{IE_1} \text{M}^+(g) \xrightarrow{\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}} \text{M}^+(aq)$$
  $$\Delta H_{\text{total}} = \Delta H_{\text{sub}} + IE_1 + \Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$$
  * Although $\text{Li}$ has the highest sublimation enthalpy and highest ionization enthalpy among alkali metals, its minute ionic radius ($r_{\text{Li}^+} = 76\text{ pm}$) generates an **enormously exothermic hydration enthalpy** ($\Delta H_{\text{hyd}} = -506\text{ kJ/mol}$).
  * This colossal energy release overcompensates for the ionization cost, making $\Delta H_{\text{total}}$ deeply negative and driving $E^\circ$ to $-3.05\text{ V}$.


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Chemical Reactivity of Alkali Metals
content:
## 2. Chemical Reactivity of Alkali Metals

### 2.1 Reactivity with Atmospheric Gases: Oxide Combustion Hierarchy
When ignited in air or excess oxygen, alkali metals exhibit a sharp divergence in oxidation products:


| Alkali Metal | Principal Combustion Product | Trace / Minor Product | Formal Oxidation State of Oxygen | Magnetic Character |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **Lithium ($\text{Li}$)** | **Normal Oxide ($\text{Li}_2\text{O}$)** | Peroxide ($\text{Li}_2\text{O}_2$) | $-2$ (Oxide ion $\text{O}^{2-}$) | Diamagnetic |
| **Sodium ($\text{Na}$)** | **Peroxide ($\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$)** | Normal Oxide ($\text{Na}_2\text{O}$) | $-1$ (Peroxide ion $\text{O}_2^{2-}$) | Diamagnetic |
| **Potassium ($\text{K}$)** | **Superoxide ($\text{KO}_2$)** | Peroxide ($\text{K}_2\text{O}_2$) | $-1/2$ (Superoxide ion $\text{O}_2^-$) | **Paramagnetic** |
| **Rubidium ($\text{Rb}$)** | **Superoxide ($\text{RbO}_2$)** | — | $-1/2$ (Superoxide ion $\text{O}_2^-$) | **Paramagnetic** |
| **Caesium ($\text{Cs}$)** | **Superoxide ($\text{CsO}_2$)** | — | $-1/2$ (Superoxide ion $\text{O}_2^-$) | **Paramagnetic** |


* **Lattice Energy Stabilization Rule:** A small cation ($\text{Li}^+$) stabilizes a small anion ($\text{O}^{2-}$), while large cations ($\text{K}^+, \text{Rb}^+, \text{Cs}^+$) with low positive charge density stabilize large, polarizable polyatomic anions ($\text{O}_2^{2-}, \text{O}_2^-$) via favorable lattice packing.
* **Hydrolysis Reactions of Oxides:**
  * Normal Oxide: $\text{Li}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{LiOH}$
  * Peroxide: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ (cold); decomposes to $\text{O}_2$ when warm.
  * Superoxide: $2\text{KO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{KOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{O}_2\uparrow$
* **Air Purification in Submarines & Space Capsules:**
  $$\mathbf{4\text{KO}_2 + 2\text{CO}_2 \to 2\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 + 3\text{O}_2\uparrow}$$
  $$\mathbf{\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \to \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\uparrow}$$
  Both $\text{KO}_2$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$ absorb respiratory $\text{CO}_2$ and regenerate life-supporting $\text{O}_2$ gas simultaneously.


---


### 2.2 Direct Nitride Formation: The Lithium Anomaly
* When heated in dry air or pure nitrogen, **Lithium is the only alkali metal that reacts directly with $\text{N}_2$** to form a stable ionic nitride:
  $$6\text{Li}(s) + \text{N}_2(g) \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{Li}_3\text{N}(s) \quad (\text{Ruby-red crystalline solid})$$
  $$\text{Li}_3\text{N} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 3\text{LiOH} + \text{NH}_3\uparrow$$
* Other alkali metals ($\text{Na, K, Rb, Cs}$) do NOT form nitrides directly because their larger cations cannot stabilize the small, triply-charged nitride anion ($\text{N}^{3-}$).


---


### 2.3 Solutions in Liquid Ammonia & Ammoniated Electrons


![Oxide-Peroxide-Superoxide Hierarchy, Liquid Ammonia, and Solvay Process](/media/oxide_superoxide_hierarchy_liquid_ammonia_and_solvay_process.webp)
*Description: Two-panel reaction chemistry and industrial process flowsheet: (A) Oxygen reactivity spectrum of alkali metals (normal oxide, peroxide, superoxide) and dissolution behavior in liquid ammonia contrasting dilute blue paramagnetic solutions with concentrated bronze diamagnetic states; (B) Step-by-step chemical flowsheet of the Solvay Ammonia-Soda process for $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$ detailing carbonation, calcination, ammonia recovery via $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, and explaining why potassium carbonate cannot be manufactured via Solvay synthesis, alongside the Castner-Kellner mercury-cell electrolysis of brine.*


* **Dissolution Phenomenon:** Alkali metals dissolve readily in liquid ammonia without hydrogen evolution to yield conducting solutions:
  $$\mathbf{\text{M} + (x + y)\text{NH}_3 \to [\text{M}(\text{NH}_3)_x]^+ + [e(\text{NH}_3)_y]^-}$$
* **Dilute Solutions ($< 3\text{ M}$):**
  * **Deep Blue Color:** Caused by light absorption in the red region ($\approx 1500\text{ nm}$) by free ammoniated electrons trapped in solvent cavities.
  * **Paramagnetic:** Presence of individual unpaired ammoniated electrons ($\mu \approx 1.73\text{ BM}$).
  * **High Electrical Conductivity:** Conduction occurs via both ammoniated cations and ammoniated electrons.
  * **Potent Reducing Agent:** Widely utilized in the Birch reduction of aromatic rings.
* **Concentrated Solutions ($> 3\text{ M}$):**
  * **Copper-Bronze Metallic Luster:** Ammoniated electrons coalesce and pair up.
  * **Diamagnetic:** Loss of paramagnetism due to electron spin-pairing: $2[e(\text{NH}_3)_y]^- \rightleftharpoons [e_2(\text{NH}_3)_{2y}]^{2-}$.
  * **Metallic Conduction:** Electrical conductivity approaches that of pure liquid metals.
* **Decomposition on Standing / Catalysis:**
  $$\text{M} + \text{NH}_3(l) \xrightarrow{\text{Fe catalyst}} \text{MNH}_2 (\text{Metal Amide}) + \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\uparrow$$


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Thermal Stability & Decomposition of Oxo-Salts
content:
## 3. Thermal Stability & Decomposition of Oxo-Salts

### 3.1 Carbonates & Bicarbonates
* **Thermal Stability of Carbonates:**
  All alkali metal carbonates are thermally stable and do not decompose below $1000^\circ\text{C}$, **except $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$**:
  $$\mathbf{\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Li}_2\text{O}(s) + \text{CO}_2\uparrow}$$
  $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3, \text{K}_2\text{CO}_3, \text{Rb}_2\text{CO}_3, \text{Cs}_2\text{CO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{No Decomposition (Melts without decomposition)}$$
  * Polarization Explanation: $\text{Li}^+$ has high polarizing power and polarizes the large $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ anion, pulling electron density toward oxygen and facilitating cleavage into $\text{Li}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CO}_2$.
* **Bicarbonates:**
  * $\text{NaHCO}_3, \text{KHCO}_3, \text{RbHCO}_3, \text{CsHCO}_3$ exist as stable crystalline solids.
  * $\text{LiHCO}_3$ is unstable and **exists only in aqueous solution**; attempting to isolate it yields $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3, \text{H}_2\text{O},$ and $\text{CO}_2$.
  * Thermal decomposition of solid sodium bicarbonate:
    $$2\text{NaHCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{> 100^\circ\text{C}} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{CO}_2(g)\uparrow$$


---


### 3.2 Nitrates
Alkali metal nitrates decompose differently upon heating:
* **Sodium, Potassium, Rubidium, Caesium Nitrates:**
  $$2\text{MNO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{500^\circ\text{C}} 2\text{MNO}_2(s) (\text{Metal Nitrite}) + \text{O}_2(g)\uparrow$$
  At higher temperatures ($> 800^\circ\text{C}$):
  $$2\text{NaNO}_2 \xrightarrow{> 800^\circ\text{C}} \text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{N}_2\uparrow + \frac{3}{2}\text{O}_2\uparrow$$
* **Lithium Nitrate Anomaly:**
  Behaves like magnesium nitrate (diagonal relationship) and decomposes to oxide and brown $\text{NO}_2$ gas:
  $$\mathbf{4\text{LiNO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{Li}_2\text{O}(s) + 4\text{NO}_2(g)\uparrow + \text{O}_2(g)\uparrow}$$


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Industrial Compounds of Sodium
content:
## 4. Industrial Compounds of Sodium

### 4.1 Sodium Hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$, Caustic Soda)
Manufactured commercially by the electrolysis of aqueous brine ($\text{NaCl}$) in the **Castner-Kellner Cell**:
* **Cathode:** Flowing liquid mercury ($\text{Hg}$).
* **Anode:** Graphite / Titanium rods.
* **Electrochemical Reactions:**
  $$\text{Anode: } 2\text{Cl}^-(aq) \to \text{Cl}_2(g)\uparrow + 2e^-$$
  $$\text{Cathode: } \text{Na}^+(aq) + e^- \xrightarrow{\text{Hg}} \text{Na-Hg} \quad (\text{Sodium Amalgam})$$
  *(Note: $\text{H}^+$ is not discharged at the mercury cathode because of its extremely high hydrogen overpotential on mercury).*
* **Decomposer Reaction:**
  $$2\text{Na-Hg} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\uparrow + 2\text{Hg}(l)\quad (\text{Hg recycled})$$
* **High-Yield Chemical Reactions of $\text{NaOH}$:**
  1. **With Halogens ($\text{Cl}_2, \text{Br}_2, \text{I}_2$):**
     * Cold & Dilute $\text{NaOH}$:
       $$2\text{NaOH} + \text{Cl}_2 \to \text{NaCl} + \text{NaOCl} (\text{Sodium Hypochlorite}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
     * Hot & Concentrated $\text{NaOH}$:
       $$6\text{NaOH} + 3\text{Cl}_2 \to 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 (\text{Sodium Chlorate}) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
  2. **With Fluorine ($\text{F}_2$):**
     * Cold & Dilute: $2\text{F}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \to 2\text{NaF} + \mathbf{\text{OF}_2\uparrow} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
     * Hot & Concentrated: $2\text{F}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \to 4\text{NaF} + \mathbf{\text{O}_2\uparrow} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$
  3. **With White Phosphorus ($\text{P}_4$):**
     $$\text{P}_4 + 3\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathbf{\text{PH}_3\uparrow} + 3\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_2 \quad (\text{Sodium Hypophosphite})$$
  4. **With Elemental Sulfur ($\text{S}_8$):**
     $$3\text{S} + 6\text{NaOH} \to 2\text{Na}_2\text{S} + \text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3 (\text{Sodium Thiosulfate / Hypo}) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
  5. **With Amphoteric Metals ($\text{Zn, Al, Be, Sn, Pb}$):**
     $$\text{Zn} + 2\text{NaOH} \to \text{Na}_2\text{ZnO}_2 (\text{Sodium Zincate}) + \text{H}_2\uparrow$$
     $$2\text{Al} + 2\text{NaOH} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{NaAlO}_2 (\text{Sodium Meta-aluminate}) + 3\text{H}_2\uparrow$$


---


### 4.2 Sodium Carbonate ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$, Washing Soda)
Manufactured via the **Solvay (Ammonia-Soda) Process**:
1. Saturation of concentrated brine with ammonia:
   $$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \to \text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$$
2. Carbonation to precipitate sparingly soluble sodium bicarbonate:
   $$\mathbf{\text{NaCl} + \text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3 \to \text{NaHCO}_3\downarrow + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}}$$
3. Calcination of $\text{NaHCO}_3$:
   $$2\text{NaHCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\uparrow + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$
4. Ammonia Recovery:
   $$\text{CaCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$$
   $$\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{Ca(OH)}_2$$
   $$2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \to 2\text{NH}_3\uparrow (\text{recycled}) + \mathbf{\text{CaCl}_2} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
* **By-Product:** Calcium chloride ($\text{CaCl}_2$).
* **Critical JEE Limitation:** Potassium carbonate ($\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$) **CANNOT** be prepared by the Solvay process because potassium bicarbonate ($\text{KHCO}_3$) is too soluble in water to precipitate upon adding $\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$ to $\text{KCl}$.
* **Efflorescence of Washing Soda:**
  $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{dry air}} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O} (\text{Monohydrate}) + 9\text{H}_2\text{O}\uparrow$$
  $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{> 373\text{ K}} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 (\text{Soda Ash, Anhydrous}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}\uparrow$$


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Group 2 Elements: Alkaline Earth Metals
content:
## 5. Group 2 Elements: Alkaline Earth Metals

### 5.1 Physical & Periodic Trends
* **General Electronic Configuration:** $[ \text{Noble Gas} ] ns^2$.
* Compared to Group 1, Group 2 elements have smaller atomic radii, higher nuclear charge, higher melting and boiling points, higher densities, and greater hardness due to two valence electrons participating in metallic bonding.
* **Ionization Enthalpies:**
  * $IE_1(\text{Group 2}) > IE_1(\text{Group 1})$ (smaller size, higher $Z_{\text{eff}}$, stable full $s^2$ subshell).
  * $IE_2(\text{Group 2}) \ll IE_2(\text{Group 1})$ (removing a second electron from Group 2 leaves a noble gas core, whereas in Group 1 it breaks a stable noble gas octet).
* **Flame Colors:**
  * **Calcium ($\text{Ca}$):** Brick Red ($622\text{ nm}$)
  * **Strontium ($\text{Sr}$):** Crimson Red ($674\text{ nm}$)
  * **Barium ($\text{Ba}$):** Apple Green ($553\text{ nm}$)
  * **Beryllium ($\text{Be}$) and Magnesium ($\text{Mg}$):** **NO FLAME COLOR** because their atomic sizes are tiny and valence electrons are bound so tightly that flame temperatures cannot excite electrons to visible emission states.


---


### 5.2 Chemical Reactivity of Alkaline Earth Metals
1. **Reactivity with Air:**
   * $\text{Be}$ and $\text{Mg}$ are kinetically inert at room temperature due to the formation of a protective, impervious oxide film.
   * When ignited, both form normal oxides ($\text{MO}$) and nitrides ($\text{M}_3\text{N}_2$):
     $$3\text{Mg} + \text{N}_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2 \quad (\text{Hydrolysis yields } 3\text{Mg(OH)}_2 + 2\text{NH}_3\uparrow)$$
   * $\text{Ba}$ forms barium peroxide ($\text{BaO}_2$).
2. **Reactivity with Water:**
   * $\text{Be}$ does not react with water or steam.
   * $\text{Mg}$ reacts only with hot water/steam: $\text{Mg} + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \to \text{MgO} + \text{H}_2\uparrow$.
   * $\text{Ca, Sr, Ba}$ react readily with cold water to evolve $\text{H}_2$ and form hydroxides.
3. **Halides & Structural Polymorphism of $\text{BeCl}_2$:**
   * Beryllium chloride ($\text{BeCl}_2$) is covalent due to high polarizing power of $\text{Be}^{2+}$.
   * **In Solid State:** Forms an infinite polymeric chlorobridged chain $(\text{BeCl}_2)_n$ where each $\text{Be}$ atom is tetrahedrally coordinated via coordinate covalent bonds ($sp^3$ hybridized).
   * **In Vapor Phase ($< 1200\text{ K}$):** Exists as a chloro-bridged planar dimer $(\text{BeCl}_2)_2$ with $sp^2$ hybridized $\text{Be}$.
   * **Above $1200\text{ K}$:** Dissociates into a linear monomer $\text{Cl}-\text{Be}-\text{Cl}$ with $sp$ hybridized $\text{Be}$.
4. **Internal Hydrolysis of Hydrated Chlorides:**
   * $\text{MgCl}_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ cannot be dehydrated by simple heating because it undergoes internal hydrolysis:
     $$\mathbf{\text{MgCl}_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{MgO} + 2\text{HCl}\uparrow + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}\uparrow}$$
   * To prepare anhydrous $\text{MgCl}_2$, it must be heated in a dry stream of $\text{HCl}$ gas, or prepared via:
     $$\text{MgO} + \text{C} + \text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{MgCl}_2 + \text{CO}\uparrow$$


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Solubility & Thermal Stability Trajectories of Group 2 Salts
content:
## 6. Solubility & Thermal Stability Trajectories of Group 2 Salts

### 6.1 Solubility Trajectories (Lattice vs. Hydration Enthalpy Competition)
Solubility in water depends on the relative magnitudes of lattice enthalpy ($U$) and hydration enthalpy ($\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$):
$$\Delta H_{\text{sol}} = U - |\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}|$$
* **Hydroxides ($\text{M(OH)}_2$):**
  $$\mathbf{\text{Solubility Order:}\quad \text{Be(OH)}_2 < \text{Mg(OH)}_2 < \text{Ca(OH)}_2 < \text{Sr(OH)}_2 < \text{Ba(OH)}_2\ (\text{Increases Down Group})}$$
  * Reason: $\text{OH}^-$ is a small anion. Lattice enthalpy ($U \propto \frac{1}{r_+ + r_-}$) decreases much faster than hydration enthalpy down the group, making dissolution progressively more exothermic.
  * Basic strength also increases: $\text{Be(OH)}_2$ (amphoteric) $\to \text{Mg(OH)}_2$ (weak base) $\to \text{Ba(OH)}_2$ (strong base).
* **Sulfates ($\text{MSO}_4$):**
  $$\mathbf{\text{Solubility Order:}\quad \text{BeSO}_4 > \text{MgSO}_4 \gg \text{CaSO}_4 > \text{SrSO}_4 > \text{BaSO}_4\ (\text{Decreases Down Group})}$$
  * Reason: $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is a large anion. The lattice enthalpy remains almost constant down the group because $r_-$ dominates $(r_+ + r_-)$. However, $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$ of the cation drops rapidly as cation size increases. Thus, hydration enthalpy fails to overcome lattice energy, making $\text{BaSO}_4$ highly insoluble.
* **Carbonates ($\text{MCO}_3$):**
  $$\mathbf{\text{Solubility Order:}\quad \text{BeCO}_3 > \text{MgCO}_3 > \text{CaCO}_3 > \text{SrCO}_3 > \text{BaCO}_3\ (\text{Decreases Down Group})}$$


---


### 6.2 Thermal Stability Trajectories of Carbonates
Thermal stability increases down the group as cation size increases:
$$\mathbf{\text{Thermal Stability:}\quad \text{BeCO}_3 < \text{MgCO}_3 < \text{CaCO}_3 < \text{SrCO}_3 < \text{BaCO}_3}$$
* $\text{BeCO}_3$ is so unstable that it decomposes at room temperature and must be preserved under an atmosphere of $\text{CO}_2$:
  $$\text{BeCO}_3 \xrightarrow{25^\circ\text{C}} \text{BeO} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow \quad (T_{\text{decomp}} \approx 100\text{ K})$$
  $$\text{BaCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{BaO} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow \quad (T_{\text{decomp}} \approx 1630\text{ K})$$


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Diagonal Relationships: $\text{Li}-\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Be}-\text{Al}$
content:
## 7. Diagonal Relationships: $\text{Li}-\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Be}-\text{Al}$

### 7.1 Visual Preservation: Diagonal Relationships & Calcium Cycle


![Diagonal Relationships and Calcium Industrial Cycle](/media/diagonal_relationships_and_calcium_industrial_cycle.webp)
*Description: Two-panel inorganic structural relationship and industrial cycle graphic: (A) Detailed side-by-side comparison of the $\text{Li}-\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Be}-\text{Al}$ diagonal relationships highlighting identical polarizing powers, shared nitride formation, carbonate thermal instability, organometallic behaviors, and carbide hydrolysis mechanisms; (B) Industrial calcium compound cycle illustrating the interconversions of $\text{CaCO}_3$ (limestone), $\text{CaO}$ (quicklime), $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ (slaked lime/lime water), calcium carbide $\text{CaC}_2$, nitrolim, and the dehydration/rehydration setting chemistry of Plaster of Paris (POP).*


---


### 7.2 The Lithium - Magnesium Diagonal Parallels
Due to nearly identical ionic radii ($\text{Li}^+ = 76\text{ pm}, \text{Mg}^{2+} = 72\text{ pm}$) and similar polarizing power:
1. **Direct Nitride Formation:** Both combine directly with nitrogen upon heating: $\text{Li}_3\text{N}$ and $\text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2$.
2. **Thermal Decomposition of Carbonates:** Both carbonates decompose on heating to give oxides and $\text{CO}_2$:
   $$\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Li}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow; \quad \text{MgCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{MgO} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$$
3. **Deliquescent Chlorides:** Both $\text{LiCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$ are deliquescent, crystallize as hydrates ($\text{LiCl} \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2 \cdot 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$), and are soluble in organic solvents (ethanol).
4. **Normal Oxides:** Both form only normal oxides ($\text{Li}_2\text{O}, \text{MgO}$) upon burning in excess air, not superoxides.
5. **Solubility of Fluorides & Phosphates:** Fluorides, carbonates, and phosphates of both elements are sparingly soluble in water.


---


### 7.3 The Beryllium - Aluminium Diagonal Parallels
Due to virtually identical charge/radius ratios ($\text{Be}^{2+} \approx 0.31 / 31\text{ pm}$, $\text{Al}^{3+} \approx 0.53 / 53\text{ pm}$):
1. **Amphoteric Oxides and Hydroxides:** Both $\text{BeO}$ and $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ dissolve in both strong acids and strong alkalis:
   $$\text{BeO} + 2\text{HCl} \to \text{BeCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}; \quad \text{BeO} + 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{Na}_2[\text{Be(OH)}_4] \quad (\text{Sodium Beryllate})$$
   $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \to 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}; \quad \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Na}[\text{Al(OH)}_4] \quad (\text{Sodium Aluminate})$$
2. **Passivation by Nitric Acid:** Both metals are rendered passive by concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ due to the instantaneous formation of an impenetrable oxide film.
3. **Chloro-Bridged Polymeric Halides:** Both $\text{BeCl}_2$ and $\text{AlCl}_3$ form chloro-bridged dimeric or polymeric structures in the vapor/solid phase with coordinate bonds, dissolve in organic solvents, and act as potent Lewis acid catalysts in Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
4. **Carbide Hydrolysis (Methanides):**
   $$\mathbf{\text{Be}_2\text{C} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Be(OH)}_2 + \text{CH}_4\uparrow}$$
   $$\mathbf{\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{Al(OH)}_3 + 3\text{CH}_4\uparrow}$$
   Both contain the methanide ion $\text{C}^{4-}$ and yield pure methane gas upon contact with water.


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — Industrial Compounds of Calcium
content:
## 8. Industrial Compounds of Calcium

### 8.1 Quicklime ($\text{CaO}$) & Slaked Lime ($\text{Ca(OH)}_2$)
1. **Quicklime ($\text{CaO}$):**
   * Prepared by calcining limestone in a rotary kiln at $1070-1270\text{ K}$:
     $$\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\uparrow \quad (\text{Reversible; } \text{CO}_2 \text{ continuously removed})$$
   * **Slaking of Lime:** Addition of limited water to quicklime produces a hissing sound, immense heat evolution, and cracks the lumps into a fine white powder of slaked lime:
     $$\mathbf{\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \to \text{Ca(OH)}_2(s) \quad (\Delta H = -63\text{ kJ/mol})}$$
   * Basic Slag Formation in Metallurgy:
     $$\text{CaO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{CaSiO}_3 (\text{Calcium Silicate Slag})$$
     $$3\text{CaO} + \text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} \to \text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2 (\text{Thomas Slag})$$
   * Carbide & Fertilizer Synthesis:
     $$\text{CaO} + 3\text{C} \xrightarrow{2000^\circ\text{C}} \text{CaC}_2 (\text{Calcium Carbide}) + \text{CO}\uparrow$$
     $$\text{CaC}_2 + \text{N}_2 \xrightarrow{1100^\circ\text{C}} \mathbf{\text{CaCN}_2 + \text{C}\quad (\text{Nitrolim Fertilizer})}$$
2. **Slaked Lime ($\text{Ca(OH)}_2$):**
   * Aqueous suspension is called **Milk of Lime**; clear filtered solution is **Lime Water**.
   * **Lime Water Test for $\text{CO}_2$:**
     $$\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \to \text{CaCO}_3\downarrow (\text{Milkiness}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
     $$\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{CO}_2(\text{excess}) + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2(aq) \quad (\text{Milkiness disappears due to soluble bicarbonate})$$
   * **Bleaching Powder Formation:**
     $$2\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + 2\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{dry, } 40^\circ\text{C}} \mathbf{\text{CaCl}_2 + \text{Ca(OCl)}_2 \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\quad (\text{Bleaching Powder})}$$


---


### 8.2 Plaster of Paris ($\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$, POP)
* **Manufacture from Gypsum:**
  Prepared by heating gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$) in a kiln carefully controlled at **$393\text{ K}\ (120^\circ\text{C})$**:
  $$\mathbf{2(\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}) \xrightarrow{393\text{ K}} 2\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\uparrow}$$
  $$\text{or}\quad \text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{393\text{ K}} \text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} + 1\frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}\uparrow$$
* **Dead Burnt Plaster Anomaly:**
  If heated above $393\text{ K}$ ($> 120^\circ\text{C}$), gypsum loses all water of crystallization to form anhydrous calcium sulfate:
  $$\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{> 393\text{ K}} \mathbf{\text{CaSO}_4 (\text{Dead Burnt Plaster})} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
  Dead burnt plaster completely loses the ability to re-hydrate and set with water!
* **Setting Mechanism of POP:**
  When mixed with water, POP forms a plastic paste that sets into a hard, rigid mass in two stages:
  1. **Setting Stage (5-15 mins):** Hemihydrate transforms into an orthorhombic dihydrate.
  2. **Hardening Stage (hours):** Orthorhombic dihydrate recrystallizes into interlocking needles of monoclinic gypsum.
  * Setting is accompanied by a **$1\%$ volume expansion**, ensuring it fills every crevice of a mold (utilized in orthopedic surgical casts, dentistry, and sculptures).


---

title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) — High-Yield JEE Problem Archetypes & Trap Logs
content:
## 10. High-Yield JEE Problem Archetypes & Trap Logs

### 10.1 Archetype 1: Action of Heat on Nitrates, Carbonates, & Oxalates
* **Nitrate Trap:**
  * Heating $\text{NaNO}_3 \to \text{NaNO}_2 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$ (No colored gas evolved).
  * Heating $\text{LiNO}_3 \to \text{Li}_2\text{O} + 2\mathbf{\text{NO}_2\uparrow}\ (\text{Brown gas}) + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$.
  * Heating $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2 \to \text{MgO} + 2\mathbf{\text{NO}_2\uparrow} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$.
* **Alkali Carbonate Trap:**
  * Only $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$ decomposes on heating to $\text{Li}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$.
  * $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ and $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$ do NOT decompose under ordinary Bunsen flame heating!


### 10.2 Archetype 2: Carbide Classification & Hydrolysis Products
* **Methanides (contain $\text{C}^{4-}$):**
  $$\text{Be}_2\text{C} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Be(OH)}_2 + \mathbf{\text{CH}_4\uparrow}$$
  $$\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{Al(OH)}_3 + 3\mathbf{\text{CH}_4\uparrow}$$
* **Acetylides (contain $\text{C}_2^{2-}$):**
  $$\text{CaC}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \mathbf{\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\uparrow}\quad (\text{Ethyne / Acetylene})$$
  $$\text{BaC}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{Ba(OH)}_2 + \mathbf{\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\uparrow}$$
* **Allylides (contain $\text{C}_3^{4-}$):**
  $$\text{Mg}_2\text{C}_3 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Mg(OH)}_2 + \mathbf{\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}\uparrow}\quad (\text{Propyne / Allylene})$$


### 10.3 Archetype 3: Disproportionation with $\text{NaOH}$
* $\text{P}_4 + 3\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{PH}_3\uparrow + 3\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_2$. Phosphorus oxidizes from $0 \to +1$ (in $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^-$) and reduces from $0 \to -3$ (in $\text{PH}_3$).
* $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH}\ (\text{cold}) \to \text{NaCl} + \text{NaOCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (Chlorine $0 \to -1$ and $0 \to +1$).
* $3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH}\ (\text{hot}) \to 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (Chlorine $0 \to -1$ and $0 \to +5$).

Chemistry Revision Context: Chapter 38 — Qualitative Cation Analysis (Basic Radicals & Systematic Inorganic Salt Analysis) **Source:** Coaching Modules & Class Notes (`scraped/Coaching_Modules/.../15. Q-Cation/Q cation-1.pdf`, `Q cation-2.pdf`, and `Qualitative Analysis (CATIONS) Theory.pdf`) **Extracted into:** `JEE/context/` **Batch:** Chemistry Inorganic Chemistry Core — Systematic Classification of Basic Radicals (Group 0 to Group VI Analytical Reagents, Selective Precipitation Principles, Solubility Product $K_{\text{sp}}$ vs. Ionic Product $Q_{\text{sp}}$, Common Ion Effect in Dilute $\text{HCl}$, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, and $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$), Group 0 ($\text{NH}_4^+$: $\text{NH}_3$ Evolution, Nessler's Reagent Synthesis, Iodide of Millon's Base $\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{Hg}-\text{O}-\text{Hg}-\text{I}$ Brown Ppt, Cobaltinitrite Test), Group I ($\text{Ag}^+, \text{Pb}^{2+}, \text{Hg}_2^{2+}$: Chloride Precipitation, Golden Rain $\text{PbI}_2$ Spangles, Chromate Reactions, Diamminesilver(I) Complexation, Mercurous Disproportionation with Ammonia), Group IIA & IIB ($\text{Hg}^{2+}, \text{Pb}^{2+}, \text{Bi}^{3+}, \text{Cu}^{2+}, \text{Cd}^{2+}$ and $\text{As}^{3+}, \text{Sb}^{3+}, \text{Sn}^{2+/4+}$: Yellow Ammonium Sulfide YAS Thiosalt Separation, Stannous Chloride Reduction of $\text{Hg}^{2+}$, Bismuth Oxychloride Turbidity, Stannite Reduction to Metallic $\text{Bi}$, Deep Blue Schweizer's Reagent $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$, Chocolate Brown Ferrocyanide, Cyanide Complexation Separation of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cd}^{2+}$), Group III ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, \text{Al}^{3+}, \text{Cr}^{3+}$: Conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ Pre-Boiling Redox Role, Prussian Blue $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$, Blood-Red $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$, Blue Lake Test for $\text{Al}^{3+}$, Thenard's Blue, Butterfly Chromium Peroxide $\text{CrO}_5$ Ethereal Layer), Group IV ($\text{Zn}^{2+}, \text{Mn}^{2+}, \text{Ni}^{2+}, \text{Co}^{2+}$: Intramolecular Hydrogen-Bonded Rosy-Red $\text{Ni(DMG)}_2$ Chelate, Vogel's Blue $[\text{Co(SCN)}_4]^{2-}$, Fischer's Salt Yellow Ppt, Rinmann's Green $\text{CoO} \cdot \text{ZnO}$, Permanganic Acid $\text{HMnO}_4$ Purple Supernatant), Group V ($\text{Ba}^{2+}, \text{Sr}^{2+}, \text{Ca}^{2+}$: Carbonate Precipitation, Acetic Acid Medium Separation, Flame Photometry), Group VI ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$: Magneson Blue Lake, White Crystalline $\text{Mg(NH}_4)\text{PO}_4 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$), and High-Yield JEE Traps (Phosphate Interference & Removal, Partial $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ Precipitation across Groups I & II). **Status:** Verified, LaTeX-Validated, and Formatted with Preserved Visual Diagrams --- ## 1. Systematic Classification of Cations & Physicochemical Principles ### 1.1 The Master Analytical Group Classification Scheme In qualitative inorganic analysis, basic radicals (cations) are classified into seven analytical groups (Group 0 to Group VI) based on the systematic differences in the solubility products ($K_{\text{sp}}$) of their insoluble chlorides, sulfides, hydroxides, carbonates, and phosphates: | Analytical Group | Cations Included | Group Reagent | Precipitated Chemical Species | Precipitate Characteristics & Colors | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **Group 0** | $\text{NH}_4^+$ | $\text{NaOH}$ or $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ (warm) | Gaseous $\text{NH}_3$ evolved | Pungent gas, turns red litmus blue, dense white fumes with $\text{HCl}$ | | **Group I** | $\text{Ag}^+, \text{Pb}^{2+}, \text{Hg}_2^{2+}$ | Dilute $\text{HCl}$ (Cold) | Chlorides: $\text{AgCl}, \text{PbCl}_2, \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ | White precipitates ($\text{PbCl}_2$ uniquely soluble in boiling water) | | **Group IIA**
*(Copper Group)* | $\text{Hg}^{2+}, \text{Pb}^{2+}, \text{Bi}^{3+}, \text{Cu}^{2+}, \text{Cd}^{2+}$ | $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas in presence of dilute $\text{HCl}$ ($0.3\text{ M}$) | Sulfides: $\text{HgS}, \text{PbS}, \text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3, \text{CuS}, \text{CdS}$ | Insoluble in Yellow Ammonium Sulfide (YAS); $\text{HgS, PbS, Bi}_2\text{S}_3, \text{CuS}$ are black; $\text{CdS}$ is canary yellow | | **Group IIB**
*(Arsenic Group)* | $\text{As}^{3+}, \text{Sb}^{3+}, \text{Sn}^{2+}, \text{Sn}^{4+}$ | $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas in presence of dilute $\text{HCl}$ ($0.3\text{ M}$) | Sulfides: $\text{As}_2\text{S}_3, \text{Sb}_2\text{S}_3, \text{SnS}, \text{SnS}_2$ | Soluble in Yellow Ammonium Sulfide (YAS); $\text{As}_2\text{S}_3$ (yellow), $\text{Sb}_2\text{S}_3$ (orange), $\text{SnS}$ (brown), $\text{SnS}_2$ (yellow) | | **Group III** | $\text{Fe}^{3+}, \text{Al}^{3+}, \text{Cr}^{3+}$ | Solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ + excess $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ (after boiling with conc. $\text{HNO}_3$) | Hydroxides: $\text{Fe(OH)}_3, \text{Al(OH)}_3, \text{Cr(OH)}_3$ | $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ (reddish-brown), $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ (gelatinous white), $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$ (green) | | **Group IV** | $\text{Zn}^{2+}, \text{Mn}^{2+}, \text{Ni}^{2+}, \text{Co}^{2+}$ | $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas in presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ | Sulfides: $\text{ZnS}, \text{MnS}, \text{NiS}, \text{CoS}$ | $\text{ZnS}$ (dirty white), $\text{MnS}$ (buff / flesh), $\text{NiS}$ (black), $\text{CoS}$ (black) | | **Group V** | $\text{Ba}^{2+}, \text{Sr}^{2+}, \text{Ca}^{2+}$ | $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ in presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ | Carbonates: $\text{BaCO}_3, \text{SrCO}_3, \text{CaCO}_3$ | All form white precipitates (separated via differential solubility in $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) | | **Group VI** | $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ | $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$ in presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ | Phosphate: $\text{Mg(NH}_4)\text{PO}_4 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ | White crystalline precipitate | --- ### 1.2 Visual Preservation: Group Separation Flowsheet & Physicochemical Laws ![Qualitative Cation Analysis Systematic Flowsheet and Group Separation](/media/qualitative_cation_analysis_systematic_flowsheet_and_group_separation.webp) *Description: Two-panel comprehensive inorganic analytical infographic: (A) Complete systematic group separation flowsheet tracing the sequential separation of cations from Group 0 through Group VI indicating specific group reagents, precipitate formulas, and characteristic precipitate colors; (B) Physical chemistry principles underlying selective precipitation: the Common Ion Effect governing sulfide precipitation in Group II vs. Group IV, hydroxide ion suppression in Group III via $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}/\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ buffer, and carbonate concentration control preventing premature precipitation of magnesium carbonate in Group V.* --- ### 1.3 Physical Chemistry Foundations of Qualitative Analysis #### 1.3.1 Precipitation Condition: Ionic Product vs. Solubility Product Precipitation of an electrolyte $\text{A}_x\text{B}_y \rightleftharpoons x\text{A}^{y+} + y\text{B}^{x-}$ occurs if and only if its ionic product ($Q_{\text{sp}}$) exceeds its thermodynamic solubility product ($K_{\text{sp}}$): $$\mathbf{Q_{\text{sp}} = [\text{A}^{y+}]^x [\text{B}^{x-}]^y > K_{\text{sp}}}$$ * If $Q_{\text{sp}} < K_{\text{sp}}$: Unsaturated solution (no precipitate forms). * If $Q_{\text{sp}} = K_{\text{sp}}$: Saturated equilibrium solution. * If $Q_{\text{sp}} > K_{\text{sp}}$: Supersaturated solution (precipitation occurs until equilibrium is restored). --- #### 1.3.2 Why Dilute $\text{HCl}$ is Chosen in Group I (Reagent Selectivity) * **Why not dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$?** If dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ were used instead of $\text{HCl}$, Group V cations ($\text{Ba}^{2+}, \text{Sr}^{2+}, \text{Ca}^{2+}$) and $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ would precipitate prematurely as insoluble sulfates ($\text{BaSO}_4, \text{SrSO}_4, \text{CaSO}_4$), hopelessly corrupting group separation. * **Why not dilute $\text{HNO}_3$?** Nitric acid forms highly water-soluble nitrate salts with all cations, resulting in zero precipitation. Furthermore, $\text{HNO}_3$ is a powerful oxidizing agent; residual $\text{HNO}_3$ carried into Group II would oxidize $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to colloidal sulfur ($\text{H}_2\text{S} + 2\text{HNO}_3 \to 2\text{NO}_2 + \text{S}\downarrow + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$), producing milky white turbidity that obscures metal sulfide detection. --- #### 1.3.3 Selective Sulfide Precipitation: Group II vs. Group IV The dissociation of hydrogen sulfide, a weak diprotic acid, proceeds in two steps: $$\text{H}_2\text{S}(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HS}^- \quad (K_{a1} \approx 10^{-7})$$ $$\text{HS}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-} \quad (K_{a2} \approx 10^{-14})$$ $$\mathbf{K_a = K_{a1} \cdot K_{a2} = \frac{[\text{H}^+]^2 [\text{S}^{2-}]}{[\text{H}_2\text{S}]} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-21}}$$ * **In Group II (Acidic Medium: $\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{dil. HCl}$):** $\text{HCl}$ is a strong acid that completely ionizes: $\text{HCl} \to \text{H}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$. By the **Common Ion Effect**, the high concentration of $[\text{H}^+]$ ($\approx 0.3\text{ M}$) suppresses the ionization of $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ overwhelmingly to the left. $$[\text{S}^{2-}] = \frac{K_a [\text{H}_2\text{S}]}{[\text{H}^+]^2} \approx \frac{(10^{-21})(0.1)}{(0.3)^2} \approx \mathbf{10^{-22}\text{ M}}$$ At this minuscule sulfide concentration, **only the cations with extremely low solubility products** ($K_{\text{sp}} \approx 10^{-30}$ to $10^{-53}$, i.e., Group II sulfides like $\text{HgS, CuS, PbS, CdS}$) exceed their $K_{\text{sp}}$ and precipitate. Group IV sulfides have significantly higher solubility products ($K_{\text{sp}} \approx 10^{-15}$ to $10^{-24}$ for $\text{ZnS, MnS, NiS, CoS}$), so their ionic product fails to reach $K_{\text{sp}}$, and they remain completely dissolved in the filtrate. * **In Group IV (Basic Medium: $\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{NH}_4\text{OH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$):** The added base $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}^+$ ions by forming water: $\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \to \text{H}_2\text{O}$. By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts dramatically to the right, elevating $[\text{S}^{2-}]$ by ten orders of magnitude ($\approx 10^{-7}\text{ M}$). Consequently, the ionic products of $\text{Zn}^{2+}, \text{Mn}^{2+}, \text{Ni}^{2+}, \text{Co}^{2+}$ easily surpass their higher $K_{\text{sp}}$ values, causing quantitative precipitation as Group IV sulfides. --- #### 1.3.4 Selective Hydroxide Precipitation: Group III vs. Group IV/V * **Role of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ before $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$:** Ammonium hydroxide is a weak base: $\text{NH}_4\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$. Adding solid ammonium chloride provides a massive concentration of the common ion $\text{NH}_4^+$ ($\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} \to \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{Cl}^-$). This common ion pushes the dissociation equilibrium back to the left, drastically depressing $[\text{OH}^-]$ to $\approx 1.5 \times 10^{-9}\text{ M}$. * Group III hydroxides have extraordinarily small solubility products: $$K_{\text{sp}}[\text{Fe(OH)}_3] \approx 3.8 \times 10^{-38}, \quad K_{\text{sp}}[\text{Al(OH)}_3] \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-33}, \quad K_{\text{sp}}[\text{Cr(OH)}_3] \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-31}$$ Thus, $Q_{\text{sp}} = [\text{M}^{3+}][\text{OH}^-]^3 > K_{\text{sp}}$, and Group III cations precipitate completely. * In contrast, Group IV and V hydroxides have much higher solubility products (e.g., $K_{\text{sp}}[\text{Zn(OH)}_2] \approx 3 \times 10^{-17}$, $K_{\text{sp}}[\text{Mg(OH)}_2] \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-11}$). Suppressed $[\text{OH}^-]$ cannot exceed their $K_{\text{sp}}$, preventing their premature precipitation in Group III. * **Why Boil with Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ Before Group III?** In the original solution, iron may be present in the ferrous state ($\text{Fe}^{2+}$). The solubility product of $\text{Fe(OH)}_2$ is relatively large ($K_{\text{sp}} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-14}$), so $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ **will NOT precipitate** with the suppressed $[\text{OH}^-]$ of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$. Boiling with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ quantitatively oxidizes $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$: $$\mathbf{6\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{HNO}_3 + 6\text{H}^+ \xrightarrow{\Delta} 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{NO}\uparrow + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ Because $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ has an ultra-low $K_{\text{sp}}$ ($3.8 \times 10^{-38}$), iron precipitates quantitatively as reddish-brown ferric hydroxide. --- #### 1.3.5 Why $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ Does Not Precipitate in Group V * Group V reagent is $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$ in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$. * The carbonate ion concentration $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$ is kept under strict control by the buffer: $$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3 + \text{HCO}_3^-$$ * This suppressed $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]$ is sufficient to exceed the low $K_{\text{sp}}$ of Group V carbonates ($K_{\text{sp}}[\text{BaCO}_3] \approx 5 \times 10^{-9}, K_{\text{sp}}[\text{SrCO}_3] \approx 1 \times 10^{-10}, K_{\text{sp}}[\text{CaCO}_3] \approx 4.8 \times 10^{-9}$), but is **insufficient to exceed the significantly higher $K_{\text{sp}}$ of magnesium carbonate** ($K_{\text{sp}}[\text{MgCO}_3] \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-5}$). * Hence, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ remains soluble and passes quantitatively into the Group VI filtrate. --- ## 2. Group 0 Cation: Ammonium ($\text{NH}_4^+$) ### 2.1 Principle & Gaseous Evolution Tests Because all ammonium salts are highly soluble in water, $\text{NH}_4^+$ cannot be precipitated by any common group reagent and is analyzed in the **original salt mixture** (zero-group analysis): 1. **Action of Strong Bases ($\text{NaOH}$ or $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$):** When heated with alkali, ammonia gas is evolved: $$\mathbf{\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{NH}_3(g)\uparrow + \text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ * Gas possesses a characteristic suffocating, pungent ammoniacal odor. * Turns moist red litmus paper blue. * Turns moist turmeric paper brown. * A glass rod dipped in concentrated $\text{HCl}$ brought near the mouth of the test tube produces **dense white fumes of ammonium chloride**: $$\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{HCl}(g) \to \mathbf{\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)\quad (\text{Dense White Fumes})}$$ * Blackens paper moistened with mercurous nitrate ($\text{Hg}_2(\text{NO}_3)_2$) due to the separation of finely divided metallic mercury: $$2\text{Hg}_2(\text{NO}_3)_2 + 4\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \mathbf{2\text{Hg}\downarrow (\text{Black})} + \text{Hg}_2\text{O} \cdot \text{Hg(NH}_2)\text{NO}_3\downarrow + 3\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$$ --- ### 2.2 Confirmatory Reaction: Nessler's Reagent Test ![Confirmatory Tests and Complexation Chemistry for Groups 4 to 6 and Zero](/media/confirmatory_tests_and_complexation_groups_4_to_6_and_zero.webp) *Description: Two-panel inorganic coordination and qualitative confirmatory graphic: (A) Groups IV & V confirmatory tests and chelation mechanisms detailing the square-planar intramolecularly hydrogen-bonded rosy-red $\text{Ni(DMG)}_2$ complex, Vogel's royal blue thiocyanate test for cobalt $[\text{Co(SCN)}_4]^{2-}$, Rinmann's green test for zinc ($\text{CoO} \cdot \text{ZnO}$), permanganic acid oxidation of manganese ($\text{HMnO}_4$), and the acetic acid separation cascade of Group V carbonates ($\text{BaCrO}_4, \text{SrSO}_4, \text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$); (B) Group VI ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$) magneson lake and ammonium phosphate precipitation, alongside Group 0 ($\text{NH}_4^+$) chemistry focusing on Nessler's reagent synthesis and the structure of the brown iodide of Millon's base.* * **Preparation of Nessler's Reagent:** Mercuric chloride solution is treated dropwise with $\text{KI}$ solution until the initial scarlet-red precipitate of $\text{HgI}_2$ completely dissolves in excess $\text{KI}$, followed by adding concentrated $\text{KOH}$ or $\text{NaOH}$: $$\text{HgCl}_2 + 2\text{KI} \to \text{HgI}_2\downarrow (\text{Scarlet Red}) + 2\text{KCl}$$ $$\text{HgI}_2 + 2\text{KI}(\text{excess}) \to \mathbf{\text{K}_2[\text{HgI}_4]\quad (\text{Potassium tetraiodomercurate(II)})}$$ $$\text{Nessler's Reagent} = \mathbf{\text{K}_2[\text{HgI}_4] + \text{KOH} \text{ (Alkaline Medium)}}$$ * **Confirmatory Reaction with $\text{NH}_3$ / $\text{NH}_4^+$:** Passing ammonia gas or adding an ammonium salt solution to Nessler's reagent produces an instantaneous **brown precipitate** (or yellow-brown coloration for trace amounts) known as the **Iodide of Millon's Base**: $$\mathbf{2\text{K}_2[\text{HgI}_4] + \text{NH}_3 + 3\text{KOH} \to \text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{Hg}-\text{O}-\text{Hg}-\text{I}\downarrow (\text{Brown Ppt}) + 7\text{KI} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ * Formula of Iodide of Millon's Base: $\mathbf{\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{Hg}-\text{O}-\text{Hg}-\text{I}}$ or $[\text{Hg}_2\text{N}]\text{I} \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O}$. --- ### 2.3 Sodium Cobaltinitrite Test Adding freshly prepared sodium hexanitrocobaltate(III) ($\text{Na}_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]$) to a neutral or slightly acidic solution of an ammonium salt produces a **canary-yellow crystalline precipitate**: $$\mathbf{3\text{NH}_4^+ + [\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]^{3-} \to (\text{NH}_4)_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]\downarrow \quad (\text{Yellow Precipitate})}$$ *(Note: $\text{K}^+$ ions also give an identical yellow precipitate of $\text{K}_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]$; hence $\text{K}^+$ must be absent).* --- ## 3. Group I Cations: $\text{Ag}^+, \text{Pb}^{2+}, \text{Hg}_2^{2+}$ (Insoluble Chlorides) ### 3.1 Initial Precipitation & Separation Strategy Addition of cold dilute $\text{HCl}$ precipitates: $$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \to \mathbf{\text{AgCl}\downarrow\ (\text{Curdy White})}$$ $$\text{Pb}^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^- \to \mathbf{\text{PbCl}_2\downarrow\ (\text{White Crystalline})}$$ $$\text{Hg}_2^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^- \to \mathbf{\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2\downarrow\ (\text{Calomel, White})}$$ * **Separation of $\text{PbCl}_2$:** The precipitate mixture is boiled with distilled water. **$\text{PbCl}_2$ dissolves completely in hot water**, whereas $\text{AgCl}$ and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ remain completely insoluble. * The hot suspension is filtered immediately: * **Filtrate:** Contains $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ ions (confirm with $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4, \text{KI},$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$). * **Residue:** Contains $\text{AgCl}$ and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$ (separated using aqueous ammonia). --- ### 3.2 Confirmatory Chemistry for Lead ($\text{Pb}^{2+}$) ![Confirmatory Tests and Chromatic Precipitates for Groups 1 to 3](/media/confirmatory_tests_and_chromatic_precipitates_groups_1_to_3.webp) *Description: Two-panel analytical reaction graphic: (A) Groups I & II confirmatory test pathways and chromatic transformations illustrating the Golden Rain spangles of $\text{PbI}_2$, yellow $\text{PbCrO}_4$ dissolving in excess alkali, curdy white $\text{AgCl}$ dissolving in ammonia, disproportionation of mercurous chloride ($\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$) to black metallic $\text{Hg}$, and the potassium cyanide separation of copper from cadmium; (B) Group III confirmatory tests illustrating Prussian Blue $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$, blood-red $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$, the aluminium blue lake test, and the ether extraction of the butterfly-structured chromium peroxide ($\text{CrO}_5$).* 1. **Recrystallization on Cooling:** As the hot $\text{PbCl}_2$ solution cools, lead chloride precipitates out as **brilliant, silky white needles**. 2. **Potassium Iodide Test — "The Golden Rain Reaction":** Adding $\text{KI}$ solution to the lead filtrate yields a bright yellow precipitate of lead iodide: $$\mathbf{\text{Pb}^{2+} + 2\text{I}^- \to \text{PbI}_2\downarrow \quad (\text{Yellow Precipitate})}$$ * **Thermal Behavior:** When the suspension is boiled with water containing a drop of acetic acid, $\text{PbI}_2$ dissolves completely to yield a colorless solution. Upon slow, quiescent cooling, it crystallizes into **magnificent, sparkling golden spangles/hexagonal plates** resembling golden rain! 3. **Potassium Chromate Test:** Adding $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ solution produces a **bright yellow precipitate of lead chromate**: $$\mathbf{\text{Pb}^{2+} + \text{CrO}_4^{2-} \to \text{PbCrO}_4\downarrow \quad (\text{Chrome Yellow})}$$ * **Amphoteric Dissolution in Excess $\text{NaOH}$:** Lead chromate is insoluble in acetic acid, but dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide to form a clear yellow solution of sodium tetrahydroxoplumbate(II): $$\text{PbCrO}_4 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{\text{Na}_2[\text{Pb(OH)}_4] + \text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4}$$ Upon re-acidifying with excess acetic acid, yellow $\text{PbCrO}_4$ reprecipitates. 4. **Sulfate Test:** Adding dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives a white precipitate of $\text{PbSO}_4$: $$\text{Pb}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-} \to \mathbf{\text{PbSO}_4\downarrow\ (\text{White})}$$ * $\text{PbSO}_4$ dissolves in ammonium acetate solution due to the formation of weakly ionized lead acetate complex: $$\text{PbSO}_4 + 2\text{CH}_3\text{COONH}_4 \to \text{Pb(CH}_3\text{COO})_2 + (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$$ --- ### 3.3 Separation of Silver ($\text{Ag}^+$) & Mercurous ($\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$) Adding warm aqueous ammonia ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$) to the residue containing $\text{AgCl}$ and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$: * **Action on Silver Chloride (Dissolution):** $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves completely by forming a stable, water-soluble coordination complex, **diamminesilver(I) chloride**: $$\mathbf{\text{AgCl}(s) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+ + \text{Cl}^-}$$ * Confirmatory Acidification: When the clear ammoniacal filtrate is acidified with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, the ammine complex is destroyed by neutralizing $\text{NH}_3$, and **curdy white $\text{AgCl}$ reprecipitates**: $$[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+ + \text{Cl}^- + 2\text{H}^+ \to \mathbf{\text{AgCl}\downarrow (\text{Curdy White})} + 2\text{NH}_4^+$$ * Confirmatory Chromate Test: Treating the ammoniacal solution with neutral $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ and acetic acid precipitates **brick-red silver chromate**: $$2\text{Ag}^+ + \text{CrO}_4^{2-} \to \mathbf{\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4\downarrow \quad (\text{Brick Red})}$$ * **Action on Mercurous Chloride (Disproportionation Blackening):** When ammonia is added to white calomel ($\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$), the solid turns **jet black** due to redox auto-disproportionation: $$\mathbf{\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2(s) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) \to \underbrace{\text{Hg}(l)}_{\text{Black Metallic}} + \underbrace{\text{Hg(NH}_2)\text{Cl}(s)}_{\text{White}} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(aq)}$$ * The resulting intimate mixture of finely divided metallic mercury ($\text{Hg}$) and insoluble mercuric amidochloride ($\text{Hg(NH}_2)\text{Cl}$) appears intensely black. * Dissolution in Aqua Regia: The black precipitate dissolves in boiling aqua regia: $$2\text{Hg} + 2\text{HNO}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \to 2\text{HgCl}_2 + 2\text{NO}\uparrow + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ $$\text{Hg(NH}_2)\text{Cl} + \text{HNO}_3 + 3\text{HCl} \to \text{HgCl}_2 + \text{N}_2\uparrow + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{HCl}$$ * Confirmation with Stannous Chloride ($\text{SnCl}_2$): Adding $\text{SnCl}_2$ dropwise to the resulting $\text{HgCl}_2$ solution yields a **silky white precipitate of $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$**, which turns **ash-grey/black** with excess $\text{SnCl}_2$ due to reduction to metallic mercury: $$2\text{HgCl}_2 + \text{SnCl}_2 \to \mathbf{\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2\downarrow (\text{Silky White})} + \text{SnCl}_4$$ $$\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2 + \text{SnCl}_2 \to \mathbf{2\text{Hg}\downarrow (\text{Grey/Black})} + \text{SnCl}_4$$ --- ## 4. Group II Cations: Copper Group (IIA) & Arsenic Group (IIB) ### 4.1 Separation of Subgroups IIA and IIB using Yellow Ammonium Sulfide (YAS) The Group II sulfide precipitate is treated with warm **Yellow Ammonium Sulfide** (YAS, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{S}_x$, containing polysulfide ions $\text{S}_2^{2-}$): * **Group IIA (Insoluble Residue):** $\text{HgS}, \text{PbS}, \text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3, \text{CuS}, \text{CdS}$ do NOT form soluble thiosalts and remain as an insoluble residue. * **Group IIB (Soluble Thiosalts):** $\text{As}_2\text{S}_3, \text{Sb}_2\text{S}_3, \text{SnS}, \text{SnS}_2$ dissolve completely via oxidation and thiosalt complexation: $$\text{As}_2\text{S}_3 + 3(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{S}_2 \to \mathbf{2(\text{NH}_4)_3\text{AsS}_4\quad (\text{Ammonium thioarsenate})} + \text{S}$$ $$\text{Sb}_2\text{S}_3 + 3(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{S}_2 \to \mathbf{2(\text{NH}_4)_3\text{SbS}_4\quad (\text{Ammonium thioantimonate})} + \text{S}$$ $$\text{SnS} + (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{S}_2 \to \mathbf{(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SnS}_3\quad (\text{Ammonium thiostannate})}$$ *(Crucial Note: $\text{SnS}$ is insoluble in colorless ammonium sulfide $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{S}$; it requires the oxidizing yellow polysulfide $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{S}_2$ to oxidize $\text{Sn(II)} \to \text{Sn(IV)}$ to form soluble thiostannate).* * **Reprecipitation of Group IIB:** When the yellow filtrate is acidified with dilute $\text{HCl}$, the thiosalts decompose, reprecipitating the higher sulfides: $$2(\text{NH}_4)_3\text{AsS}_4 + 6\text{HCl} \to \mathbf{\text{As}_2\text{S}_5\downarrow (\text{Yellow})} + 6\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + 3\text{H}_2\text{S}\uparrow$$ $$2(\text{NH}_4)_3\text{SbS}_4 + 6\text{HCl} \to \mathbf{\text{Sb}_2\text{S}_5\downarrow (\text{Orange})} + 6\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + 3\text{H}_2\text{S}\uparrow$$ $$(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SnS}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \to \mathbf{\text{SnS}_2\downarrow (\text{Yellow})} + 2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{S}\uparrow$$ --- ### 4.2 Group IIA Systematic Analysis & Confirmatory Chemistry The insoluble IIA residue ($\text{HgS, PbS, Bi}_2\text{S}_3, \text{CuS, CdS}$) is boiled with **dilute nitric acid ($50\%\ \text{HNO}_3$, $1:1$ ratio)**: * **$\text{HgS}$ is completely insoluble in dilute $\text{HNO}_3$** due to its exceptionally low solubility product ($K_{\text{sp}} \approx 10^{-53}$). It remains as a black residue. * $\text{PbS, Bi}_2\text{S}_3, \text{CuS,}$ and $\text{CdS}$ dissolve in dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, evolving $\text{NO}$ gas: $$3\text{CuS} + 8\text{HNO}_3 \to 3\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + 3\text{S}\downarrow + 2\text{NO}\uparrow + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ #### 4.2.1 Mercury(II) ($\text{Hg}^{2+}$) Confirmation * The black $\text{HgS}$ residue dissolves in fresh **aqua regia** ($3\text{ HCl} : 1\text{ HNO}_3$): $$3\text{HgS} + 2\text{HNO}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \to 3\text{HgCl}_2 + 3\text{S}\downarrow + 2\text{NO}\uparrow + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ * Dilute with water, boil off excess chlorine, and test: * **$\text{SnCl}_2$ Test:** White silky $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2 \to$ grey/black metallic $\text{Hg}$. * **Copper Coin Test:** A clean copper strip immersed in $\text{HgCl}_2$ solution becomes coated with a silvery-white film of mercury amalgam: $\text{HgCl}_2 + \text{Cu} \to \text{CuCl}_2 + \text{Hg}$ (shines like silver when rubbed). * **Potassium Iodide Test:** Adding $\text{KI}$ dropwise yields a **scarlet-red precipitate of $\text{HgI}_2$**, which dissolves in excess $\text{KI}$ to form colorless Nessler's complex $[\text{HgI}_4]^{2-}$: $$\text{Hg}^{2+} + 2\text{I}^- \to \mathbf{\text{HgI}_2\downarrow \quad (\text{Scarlet Red})}$$ $$\text{HgI}_2 + 2\text{I}^-(\text{excess}) \to \mathbf{[\text{HgI}_4]^{2-}\quad (\text{Colorless Soluble Complex})}$$ #### 4.2.2 Separation of Lead ($\text{Pb}^{2+}$) * To the nitric acid solution, add dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and alcohol. $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ precipitates as white $\text{PbSO}_4$, which is filtered off and confirmed as described in Group I. #### 4.2.3 Bismuth ($\text{Bi}^{3+}$) Confirmation * To the filtrate containing $\text{Bi}^{3+}, \text{Cu}^{2+}, \text{Cd}^{2+}$, add excess aqueous ammonia ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$): * **$\text{Bi}^{3+}$ precipitates as white gelatinous $\text{Bi(OH)}_3$**. * $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cd}^{2+}$ dissolve as soluble tetraammine complexes. * **Sodium Stannite Reduction:** Filter the white $\text{Bi(OH)}_3$ precipitate and pour freshly prepared sodium stannite solution over it. Instantaneous reduction yields **jet-black metallic bismuth**: $$\text{SnCl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \to \text{Sn(OH)}_2\downarrow + 2\text{NaCl}$$ $$\text{Sn(OH)}_2 + 2\text{NaOH}(\text{excess}) \to \mathbf{\text{Na}_2\text{SnO}_2\quad (\text{Sodium Stannite})} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ $$\mathbf{2\text{Bi(OH)}_3(s) + 3\text{Na}_2\text{SnO}_2(aq) \to 2\text{Bi}(s)\downarrow (\text{Jet Black}) + 3\text{Na}_2\text{SnO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ * **Water Hydrolysis Test:** Dissolving $\text{Bi(OH)}_3$ in minimum dilute $\text{HCl}$ yields $\text{BiCl}_3$. Pouring this into a large excess of water causes extensive hydrolysis, precipitating **white milky bismuth oxychloride**: $$\mathbf{\text{BiCl}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{BiOCl}\downarrow (\text{Bismuthyl Chloride / Pearl White}) + 2\text{HCl}}$$ #### 4.2.4 Separation of Copper ($\text{Cu}^{2+}$) & Cadmium ($\text{Cd}^{2+}$) The ammoniacal filtrate contains $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ (intense azure blue) and $[\text{Cd(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ (colorless): 1. **Copper Confirmation via Ferrocyanide:** Acidify a portion with acetic acid and add potassium ferrocyanide ($\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$). An intense **chocolate-brown precipitate of cupric ferrocyanide** forms: $$\mathbf{2\text{Cu}^{2+} + [\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-} \to \text{Cu}_2[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]\downarrow \quad (\text{Chocolate Brown})}$$ 2. **Cyanide Complexation Separation Method:** To the blue ammoniacal solution, add potassium cyanide ($\text{KCN}$) dropwise until the blue color completely discharges: $$2[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+} + 10\text{CN}^- \to 2[\text{Cu(CN)}_4]^{3-} + (\text{CN})_2\uparrow (\text{Cyanogen Gas}) + 8\text{NH}_3$$ $$[\text{Cd(NH}_3)_4]^{2+} + 4\text{CN}^- \to [\text{Cd(CN)}_4]^{2-} + 4\text{NH}_3$$ * In $[\text{Cu(CN)}_4]^{3-}$, copper has been reduced to $\text{Cu(I)}$; this tetracyanocuprate(I) complex has an astronomical formation constant ($K_f \approx 10^{28}$) and furnishes virtually zero free $\text{Cu}^+$ ions. * In $[\text{Cd(CN)}_4]^{2-}$, cadmium remains $\text{Cd(II)}$; this complex is significantly less stable ($K_f \approx 10^{17}$) and maintains an appreciable equilibrium concentration of $\text{Cd}^{2+}$. * **Passing $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ Gas:** * $[\text{Cu(CN)}_4]^{3-}$ gives **NO PRECIPITATE**. * $[\text{Cd(CN)}_4]^{2-}$ decomposes, precipitating a **brilliant canary-yellow precipitate of Cadmium Sulfide ($\text{CdS}$)**: $$\mathbf{[\text{Cd(CN)}_4]^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{S} \to \text{CdS}\downarrow (\text{Canary Yellow}) + 2\text{H}^+ + 4\text{CN}^-}$$ --- ## 5. Group III Cations: $\text{Fe}^{3+}, \text{Al}^{3+}, \text{Cr}^{3+}$ (Insoluble Hydroxides) ### 5.1 Separation of Group III Hydroxides The Group III hydroxide precipitate ($\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ reddish-brown, $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ gelatinous white, $\text{Cr(OH)}_3$ green) is treated with **excess $\text{NaOH}$ and $3\%\ \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ (or sodium peroxide $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$)**, followed by boiling: * **$\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ is basic:** It does NOT dissolve in $\text{NaOH}$ and remains as a reddish-brown residue. * **$\text{Al(OH)}_3$ is amphoteric:** It dissolves to form colorless soluble sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate: $$\text{Al(OH)}_3(s) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \to \mathbf{\text{Na}[\text{Al(OH)}_4](aq)\quad (\text{Colorless Solution})}$$ * **$\text{Cr(OH)}_3$ is amphoteric and oxidizable:** It oxidizes from $\text{Cr(III)}$ to $\text{Cr(VI)}$, dissolving to form **bright yellow sodium chromate**: $$\mathbf{2\text{Cr(OH)}_3(s) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \to 2\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4(aq) (\text{Bright Yellow}) + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ --- ### 5.2 Iron ($\text{Fe}^{3+}$) Confirmatory Chemistry Dissolve the reddish-brown $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ residue in dilute $\text{HCl}$ to obtain yellow $\text{FeCl}_3$: 1. **Prussian Blue Reaction:** Adding potassium ferrocyanide ($\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$) produces an intense, deep **Prussian Blue precipitate/colloid of ferric ferrocyanide**: $$\mathbf{4\text{Fe}^{3+} + 3[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-} \to \text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3\downarrow \quad (\text{Prussian Blue})}$$ * Excess alkali decomposes Prussian blue: $$\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3 + 12\text{NaOH} \to 4\text{Fe(OH)}_3\downarrow (\text{Reddish-Brown}) + 3\text{Na}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$$ 2. **Potassium Thiocyanate (KCNS) Reaction:** Adding $\text{KCNS}$ or $\text{NH}_4\text{SCN}$ produces an intense **blood-red coloration** due to pentaaquathiocyanatoiron(III) complex: $$\mathbf{\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{SCN}^- + 5\text{H}_2\text{O} \to [\text{Fe(SCN)}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5]^{2+}\quad (\text{Blood Red Coloration})}$$ * The blood-red color is discharged by adding sodium fluoride ($\text{NaF}$) or mercuric chloride ($\text{HgCl}_2$) due to the formation of colorless, highly stable $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$ or un-ionized $\text{Hg(SCN)}_2$. 3. **Turnbull's Blue vs. Prussian Blue Distinction:** * $\text{Fe}^{3+} + [\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-} \to \text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$ (Prussian Blue). * $\text{Fe}^{2+} + [\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-} \to \text{Fe}_3[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_2$ (Turnbull's Blue). * Both compounds are now known to be structurally identical coordination polymers containing mixed-valence $\text{Fe(II)}-\text{CN}-\text{Fe(III)}$ networks! --- ### 5.3 Aluminium ($\text{Al}^{3+}$) Confirmatory Chemistry 1. **Reprecipitation via Ammonium Chloride:** Boiling the colorless sodium aluminate filtrate with solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ neutralizes the caustic alkali and **reprecipitates gelatinous white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$**: $$\mathbf{\text{Na}[\text{Al(OH)}_4] + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Al(OH)}_3\downarrow (\text{Gelatinous White}) + \text{NaCl} + \text{NH}_3\uparrow + \text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ 2. **The Blue Lake Test:** * Dissolve the white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ precipitate in dilute $\text{HCl}$. * Add 1-2 drops of blue litmus solution (which turns red in the acidic solution). * Add $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ dropwise down the side of the test tube. * A **brilliant blue floating precipitate / lake** forms suspended in the upper alkaline zone with a clear liquid beneath. * Mechanism: Freshly precipitated colloidal $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ has an enormous surface area that strongly adsorbs the blue litmus dye anion! 3. **Cobalt Nitrate Test (Thenard's Blue):** Heating $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ with a drop of cobalt nitrate ($\text{Co(NO}_3)_2$) on a charcoal block gives an intensely blue, non-fusible mass of cobalt meta-aluminate: $$2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Co(NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathbf{2(\text{CoO} \cdot \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3)\quad (\text{Thenard's Blue})} + 4\text{NO}_2\uparrow + \text{O}_2\uparrow$$ --- ### 5.4 Chromium ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$) Confirmatory Chemistry 1. **Lead Chromate Test:** Acidify the yellow sodium chromate filtrate with acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) and add lead acetate solution. A **bright yellow precipitate of lead chromate** forms: $$\mathbf{\text{Pb}^{2+} + \text{CrO}_4^{2-} \to \text{PbCrO}_4\downarrow \quad (\text{Chrome Yellow})}$$ 2. **Chromium Peroxide Butterfly Test ($\text{CrO}_5$):** * Acidify the chromate solution with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. * Add $1-2\text{ mL}$ of amyl alcohol or diethyl ether. * Add $3\%\ \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ and shake gently. * The organic layer extracts a magnificent, **intense royal-blue compound: Chromium Peroxide ($\text{CrO}_5$)**: $$\mathbf{\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+ + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{CrO}_5 + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ * **Molecular Structure:** $\text{CrO}_5$ possesses a **butterfly structure** containing one oxo oxygen ($=\text{O}$) and two peroxo bridges ($-\text{O}-\text{O}-$). The formal oxidation state of chromium is **$+6$**: $$\text{Cr}(=\text{O})(\text{O}_2)_2$$ * In water, $\text{CrO}_5$ rapidly decomposes to green $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ and $\text{O}_2$, but is stabilized in coordinating donor solvents (ether, pyridine, amyl alcohol). --- ## 6. Group IV Cations: $\text{Zn}^{2+}, \text{Mn}^{2+}, \text{Ni}^{2+}, \text{Co}^{2+}$ (Insoluble Sulfides in Basic Medium) ### 6.1 Nickel ($\text{Ni}^{2+}$) Confirmatory Chemistry Dissolve the black $\text{NiS}$ precipitate in aqua regia, neutralize with $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, and perform: * **The Dimethylglyoxime (DMG) Test:** Adding an ethanolic solution of dimethylglyoxime (DMG) in the presence of excess $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ produces a voluminous, **brilliant scarlet / rosy-red precipitate**: $$\mathbf{\text{Ni}^{2+} + 2\text{DMG} + 2\text{NH}_4\text{OH} \to [\text{Ni(DMG)}_2]\downarrow (\text{Rosy Red}) + 2\text{NH}_4^+ + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ * **Structural Highlights of $[\text{Ni(DMG)}_2]$:** * **Geometry:** Square planar, $dsp^2$ hybridized, **diamagnetic** ($d^8$ low spin configuration induced by strong chelation). * **Hydrogen Bonding:** Stabilized by **two symmetrical intramolecular $\text{O}-\text{H}\cdots \text{O}$ hydrogen bonds**, creating four fused chelate rings (two 5-membered rings coordinating $\text{Ni}$ to nitrogens, and two 6-membered hydrogen-bonded rings). * The complex is neutral, hydrophobic, and exceptionally insoluble in aqueous ammonia. --- ### 6.2 Cobalt ($\text{Co}^{2+}$) Confirmatory Chemistry Dissolve the black $\text{CoS}$ precipitate in aqua regia and test: 1. **Vogel's Thiocyanate Test:** Add ammonium thiocyanate ($\text{NH}_4\text{SCN}$) and $1\text{ mL}$ of amyl alcohol (or acetone / ether) and shake. An **intense royal-blue color** appears in the organic layer: $$\mathbf{\text{Co}^{2+} + 4\text{SCN}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{Co(SCN)}_4]^{2-}\quad (\text{Tetrathiocyanatocobaltate(II), Royal Blue})}$$ * The tetrahedral complex $[\text{Co(SCN)}_4]^{2-}$ is unstable in water (pink due to $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$), but is stabilized and extracted quantitatively into less polar oxygenated organic solvents. 2. **Fischer's Salt Reaction (Potassium Hexanitrocobaltate(III)):** Add potassium nitrite ($\text{KNO}_2$) in excess after acidifying with acetic acid. An intense **canary-yellow crystalline precipitate of Fischer's Salt** forms: $$\text{Co}^{2+} + \text{NO}_2^- + 2\text{H}^+ \to \text{Co}^{3+} + \text{NO}\uparrow + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ $$\mathbf{\text{Co}^{3+} + 3\text{K}^+ + 6\text{NO}_2^- \to \text{K}_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]\downarrow \quad (\text{Fischer's Salt, Yellow Crystalline})}$$ --- ### 6.3 Zinc ($\text{Zn}^{2+}$) Confirmatory Chemistry Dissolve the dirty-white $\text{ZnS}$ precipitate in dilute $\text{HCl}$: 1. **Action of Sodium Hydroxide:** Adding $\text{NaOH}$ gives a white gelatinous precipitate of $\text{Zn(OH)}_2$, which dissolves completely in excess $\text{NaOH}$ to yield colorless sodium zincate: $$\text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\text{NaOH} \to \text{Zn(OH)}_2\downarrow + 2\text{Na}^+$$ $$\text{Zn(OH)}_2 + 2\text{NaOH}(\text{excess}) \to \mathbf{\text{Na}_2[\text{Zn(OH)}_4]\quad (\text{Sodium Zincate})}$$ * Passing $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ into this alkaline zincate solution reprecipitates white $\text{ZnS}$. 2. **Rinmann's Green Test:** Moisten the zinc salt on a charcoal block with a dilute drop of cobalt nitrate ($\text{Co(NO}_3)_2$) and heat strongly in an oxidizing blowpipe flame: $$\text{ZnSO}_4 + \text{Co(NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathbf{\text{CoO} \cdot \text{ZnO}\quad (\text{Rinmann's Green / Cobalt Zincate})} + \text{SO}_3 + 2\text{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$$ --- ### 6.4 Manganese ($\text{Mn}^{2+}$) Confirmatory Chemistry Dissolve the flesh/buff-colored $\text{MnS}$ precipitate in dilute $\text{HCl}$ and boil off $\text{H}_2\text{S}$: 1. **Oxidation to Permanganic Acid ($\text{PbO}_2$ Test):** Boil the manganese solution with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ and a pinch of solid lead dioxide ($\text{PbO}_2$, or sodium bismuthate $\text{NaBiO}_3$). Allow the excess brown $\text{PbO}_2$ to settle: $$\mathbf{2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\text{PbO}_2(s) + 4\text{H}^+ \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{HMnO}_4(aq) (\text{Intense Purple / Pink}) + 5\text{Pb}^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ * The supernatant turns a characteristic **vibrant pink/purple color** due to permanganic acid ($\text{MnO}_4^-$). * Note: $\text{HCl}$ must be completely absent because chloride ions reduce $\text{MnO}_4^-$ to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ while oxidizing to $\text{Cl}_2$. --- ## 7. Group V Cations: $\text{Ba}^{2+}, \text{Sr}^{2+}, \text{Ca}^{2+}$ (Insoluble Carbonates) ### 7.1 Separation Cascade in Acetic Acid Medium The white carbonate precipitate ($\text{BaCO}_3, \text{SrCO}_3, \text{CaCO}_3$) is dissolved in minimum hot dilute **acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$)**: 1. **Barium ($\text{Ba}^{2+}$) Precipitation:** Add potassium chromate ($\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$) solution. **$\text{BaCrO}_4$ precipitates as a pale yellow solid**, while $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ remain completely dissolved because strontium and calcium chromates are soluble in dilute acetic acid: $$\mathbf{\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{CrO}_4^{2-} \to \text{BaCrO}_4\downarrow \quad (\text{Yellow Precipitate, Insoluble in Acetic Acid})}$$ 2. **Strontium ($\text{Sr}^{2+}$) Precipitation:** Filter off $\text{BaCrO}_4$. Make the filtrate ammoniacal and add saturated ammonium sulfate ($(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$) solution and warm. **$\text{SrSO}_4$ precipitates as a white solid**, while $\text{CaSO}_4$ remains in solution: $$\mathbf{\text{Sr}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-} \to \text{SrSO}_4\downarrow \quad (\text{White Precipitate})}$$ 3. **Calcium ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$) Precipitation:** Filter off $\text{SrSO}_4$. To the filtrate, add ammonium oxalate ($(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$). **$\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ precipitates as a fine white crystalline solid**: $$\mathbf{\text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \to \text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4\downarrow \quad (\text{Calcium Oxalate, White Precipitate})}$$ --- ### 7.2 Flame Test Identification * **Barium ($\text{Ba}^{2+}$):** Persistent **Apple Green / Grassy Green** flame ($553.5\text{ nm}$). * **Strontium ($\text{Sr}^{2+}$):** Persistent **Crimson Red** flame ($674.4\text{ nm}$). * **Calcium ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$):** Flashing **Brick Red** flame ($622.0\text{ nm}$, seen through cobalt blue glass as light green). --- ## 8. Group VI Cation: Magnesium ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$) ### 8.1 Disodium Hydrogen Phosphate Test To the filtrate from Group V, add disodium hydrogen phosphate ($\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$) in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and concentrated $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$, and scratch the inner wall of the test tube with a glass rod: $$\mathbf{\text{Mg}^{2+} + \text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4 + \text{NH}_4\text{OH} \to \text{Mg(NH}_4)\text{PO}_4 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}\downarrow (\text{White Crystalline}) + 2\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ * Forms a characteristic **white crystalline precipitate of magnesium ammonium phosphate**. * Ignition of the dried precipitate yields magnesium pyrophosphate: $$2\text{Mg(NH}_4)\text{PO}_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathbf{\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\text{NH}_3\uparrow + \text{H}_2\text{O}}$$ --- ### 8.2 Magneson Reagent Test Add a few drops of **Magneson I** (4-(4-nitrophenylazo)resorcinol) or Magneson II to the magnesium solution, followed by excess $\text{NaOH}$: * Forms a magnificent **sky-blue precipitate / blue lake** due to dye adsorption on colloidal $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$. --- ### 8.3 Cobalt Nitrate Test Heating magnesium salts with cobalt nitrate on a charcoal cavity gives a **pale pink / flesh-colored non-fusible mass ($\text{CoO} \cdot \text{MgO}$)**. --- ## 9. ($\text{SnCl}_2$) | $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2 \to \text{Hg}$ | **Silky white $\to$ ash grey/black metallic mercury** | | $\text{Hg}^{2+}$ | Potassium Iodide ($\text{KI}$) | $\text{HgI}_2 \to \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ | $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ lake | **Blue floating lake suspended in clear liquid** | | $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ | $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{ether}$ | $\text{CrO}_5$ | **Intense royal-blue ethereal layer (butterfly structure)** | | $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ | Dimethylglyoxime $+ \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ | $[\text{Ni(DMG)}_2]$ | **Brilliant Rosy-Red precipitate (square planar, diamagnetic)** | | $\text{Co}^{2+}$ | $\text{NH}_4\text{SCN} + \text{amyl alcohol}$ | $[\text{Co(SCN)}_4]^{2-}$ | **Royal-blue organic layer (Vogel's reaction)** | | $\text{Co}^{2+}$ | $\text{KNO}_2 + | **Rinmann's Green non-fusible mass** | | $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ | $\text{PbO}_2 + \text{conc. HNO}_3$ + heat | $\text{HMnO}_4$ | **Intense purple/pink supernatant** | | $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ | $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ | $\text{BaCrO}_4$ | **Yellow precipitate; Apple-green flame** | | $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ | $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$ | $\text{SrSO}_4$ | **White precipitate; Crimson-red flame** | | $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ | $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ | $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ | **White precipitate; Brick-red flame** | | $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ | $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4 + \text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ | $\text{Mg(NH}_4)\text{PO}_4 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ | **White crystalline precipitate** | | $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ | Magneson reagent $+ \text{NaOH}$ | $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ lake | **Sky-blue precipitate / lake** | --- ### 9.2 High-Yield Exam Traps & Conceptual Pitfalls #### Trap 1: Interference of Phosphate ($\text{PO}_4^{3-}$) and Interfering Acid Radicals * Phosphates, borates, oxalates, and fluorides of alkaline earth metals and Group IV metals are insoluble in neutral or alkaline media, but soluble in acidic media. * When $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is added to precipitate Group III in the presence of $\text{PO}_4^{3-}$, the medium becomes alkaline, causing **premature precipitation of $\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2, \text{Ba}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2, \text{Sr}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2, \text{Mg}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$ alongside $\text{Fe(OH)}_3$ in Group III**! * **Remedy (Phosphate Removal Scheme):** After Group II, boil off $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, test for phosphate with ammonium molybdate. If present, add $\text{FeCl}_3$ in the presence of sodium acetate buffer ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$). Ferric phosphate ($\text{FePO}_4$) precipitates as an insoluble yellowish-white solid and is filtered off before proceeding to Group III! #### Trap 2: Why Does $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ Appear in Both Group I and Group II? * The solubility product of lead chloride ($\text{PbCl}_2$) is moderately high ($K_{\text{sp}} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-5}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$). * In Group I, cold dilute $\text{HCl}$ does not precipitate lead quantitatively; an appreciable concentration of $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ remains dissolved in the filtrate. * When $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ is passed in Group II, because $K_{\text{sp}}[\text{PbS}] \approx 10^{-28}$ is vastly lower than $K_{\text{sp}}[\text{PbCl}_2]$, the residual lead precipitates quantitatively as black $\text{PbS}$. #### Trap 3: Oxidation State & Disproportionation Traps in Mercury * $\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$ (mercurous) contains a metal-metal bond with single unpaired electrons paired up: $^+\text{Hg}-\text{Hg}^+$ (diamagnetic). * When treated with $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$ auto-disproportionates into elemental $\text{Hg}^0$ (black) and $\text{Hg}^{2+}$ (white $\text{Hg(NH}_2)\text{Cl}$). * When treated with $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$ yields black $\text{HgS} + \text{Hg}$.
