2. Boron & Its High-Yield Compounds
![Diborane 3c2e Bonding And Borax Structure](/media/diborane_3c2e_bonding_and_borax_structure.webp) Description: Two-panel reference diagram: (Panel A) Diborane ($B_2H_6$) showing four terminal 2c-2e $B-H_t$ covalent bonds and two 3c-2e banana bridges ($B-H_b-B$) with bond angles and lengths; (Panel B) Borax core anion $[B_4O_5(OH)_4]^{2-}$ illustrating two tetrahedral $sp^3$ boron centers and two planar $sp^2$ boron centers bridged by five $B-O-B$ linkages.
2.1 Diborane ($\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$)
1. Synthesis Pathways:
   * Industrial method (reduction of boron trifluoride by sodium hydride): $$2\text{BF}_3 + 6\text{NaH} \xrightarrow{450\text{ K}} \text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 6\text{NaF}$$
   * Laboratory preparation: $$4\text{BCl}_3 + 3\text{LiAlH}_4 \xrightarrow{\text{Dry Ether}} 2\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 3\text{LiCl} + 3\text{AlCl}_3$$ $$2\text{NaBH}_4 + \text{I}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Diglyme}} \text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 2\text{NaI} + \text{H}_2 \uparrow$$
2. Molecular Geometry & Electronic Structure:
   * Contains 12 valence electrons (3 from each of two Borons, 1 from each of six Hydrogens). Monomeric $\text{BH}_3$ has only 6 electrons and is electron-deficient.
   * Four terminal Hydrogens ($\text{H}_t$) form classical two-center two-electron ($2c-2e$) bonds: length $= 1.19\text{ \AA}$, $\angle \text{H}_t-\text{B}-\text{H}_t = 120^\circ$.
   * Two bridging Hydrogens ($\text{H}_b$) lie above and below the molecular plane, forming three-center two-electron ($3c-2e$) "banana" bonds: length $= 1.31\text{ \AA}$, $\angle \text{B}-\text{H}_b-\text{B} = 97^\circ$.
   * Both Boron atoms are $sp^3$ hybridized.
3. Key Chemical Reactions:
   * Combustion (Extremely Exothermic): $$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 3\text{O}_2 \longrightarrow \text{B}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \quad (\Delta H = -1976\text{ kJ/mol})$$
   * Hydrolysis: $$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 + 6\text{H}_2 \uparrow$$
   * Reaction with Alcohol: $$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 6\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \longrightarrow 2\text{B}(\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5)_3 + 6\text{H}_2 \uparrow$$ (Triethyl borate burns with a characteristic green-edged flame).
   * Cleavage Reactions with Lewis Bases:
      * Symmetrical Cleavage (Large/Soft bases: $\text{CO}, \text{Me}_3\text{N}, \text{THF}, \text{R}_2\text{S}$): $$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 2\text{NMe}_3 \longrightarrow 2[\text{Me}_3\text{N} \to \text{BH}_3]$$ $$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 2\text{CO} \longrightarrow 2[\text{OC} \to \text{BH}_3]$$
      * Unsymmetrical Cleavage (Small/Hard bases: $\text{NH}_3, \text{MeNH}_2, \text{Me}_2\text{NH}$): $$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 2\text{NH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Low Temp}} [\text{BH}_2(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+ [\text{BH}_4]^-$$
2.2 Borazole / Inorganic Benzene ($\text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_6$)
* Synthesis: Heating the unsymmetrical cleavage adduct at $200^\circ\text{C}$: $$3\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 6\text{NH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2\text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_6 + 12\text{H}_2 \uparrow$$ $$3\text{BCl}_3 + 3\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} \longrightarrow \text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_3\text{Cl}_3 + 9\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_6$$
* Structure & Comparison with Benzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$):
   * Hexagonal planar ring with alternating $\text{B}$ and $\text{N}$ atoms; both $\text{B}$ and $\text{N}$ are $sp^2$ hybridized.
   * Isoelectronic and isostructural with benzene, containing $6\pi$ delocalized electrons.
   * Differences: Due to electronegativity difference ($\chi_{\text{N}} > \chi_{\text{B}}$), the $\text{B}-\text{N}$ bond is polar ($\text{B}^{\delta+} - \text{N}^{\delta-}$).
   * Reactivity: Borazole undergoes electrophilic and nucleophilic additions much more readily than benzene.
      * Addition of $\text{HCl}$: $$\text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_6 + 3\text{HCl} \longrightarrow \text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_9\text{Cl}_3$$ (Hydrogen adds to more electronegative Nitrogen; Chlorine adds to Boron).
      * Hydrolysis: $$\text{B}_3\text{N}_3\text{H}_6 + 9\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 3\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 + 3\text{NH}_3 + 3\text{H}_2 \uparrow$$
2.3 Borax ($\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$)
* True Structural Formula: $\mathbf{\text{Na}_2[\text{B}_4\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4] \cdot 8\text{H}_2\text{O}}$.
   * Contains a bicyclic core consisting of two tetrahedral $\text{BO}_4$ units ($sp^3$ hybridized, formal charge $-1$) and two triangular planar $\text{BO}_3$ units ($sp^2$ hybridized, neutral).
   * Number of $\text{B}-\text{O}-\text{B}$ linkages $= 5$.
   * Number of $\text{B}-\text{OH}$ units $= 4$.
* Aqueous Chemistry: $$\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 + 7\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NaOH} + 4\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$$
   * Forms a buffer solution of a strong base ($\text{NaOH}$) and a weak acid ($\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$); hence its aqueous solution is alkaline ($\text{pH} > 7$).
* Borax Bead Test: $$\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \xrightarrow{\text{Red Heat}} \underbrace{2\text{NaBO}_2 + \text{B}_2\text{O}3}{\text{Transparent Glassy Bead}}$$
   * When heated with colored transition metal salts, forms characteristic metaborates:
      * Cobalt ($\text{Co}^{2+}$): $\text{Co}(\text{BO}_2)_2$ $\to$ Deep Blue (in both oxidizing and reducing flames).
      * Copper ($\text{Cu}^{2+}$): $\text{Cu}(\text{BO}_2)_2$ $\to$ Blue-Green (oxidizing flame), turns red opaque ($\text{Cu}$) in reducing flame.
      * Chromium ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$): $\text{Cr}(\text{BO}_2)_3$ $\to$ Green.
      * Iron ($\text{Fe}^{3+}$): $\text{Fe}(\text{BO}_2)_3$ $\to$ Yellow/Brown.
2.4 Orthoboric Acid ($\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ or $\text{B}(\text{OH})_3$)
* Acidic Nature:
   * It is not a protonic acid (does not donate $\text{H}^+$ by itself).
   * It acts as a weak, monobasic Lewis acid by accepting an electron pair from the $\text{OH}^-$ of a water molecule: $$\text{B}(\text{OH})_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons [\text{B}(\text{OH})_4]^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ \quad (\text{p}K_a = 9.25)$$
* Titration with $\text{NaOH}$ & Polyhydroxy Activation:
   * Cannot be directly titrated with $\text{NaOH}$ using phenolphthalein because its dissociation constant is too small.
   * In the presence of cis-polyols (glycerol, mannitol, catechol, sugars), it forms stable, rigid cyclic chelate complexes with $[\text{B}(\text{OH})_4]^-$, shifting the equilibrium forward and converting it into a strong monobasic acid that can be titrated quantitatively with phenolphthalein.
* Thermal Decomposition: $$\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 \xrightarrow{373\text{ K}} \text{HBO}_2 \text{ (Metaboric acid)} \xrightarrow{413\text{ K}} \text{H}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \text{ (Tetraboric acid)} \xrightarrow{\text{Red Heat}} \text{B}_2\text{O}_3 \text{ (Boric oxide)}$$
2.5 Boron Trihalides ($\text{BX}_3$) & Back-Bonding
* Lewis Acidity Order: $$\mathbf{\text{BF}_3 < \text{BCl}_3 < \text{BBr}_3 < \text{BI}_3}$$
* Explanation:
   * Boron has an empty $2p$ orbital in planar $sp^2$ hybridized $\text{BX}_3$.
   * Halogens donate lone pairs from their filled $np$ orbitals into Boron's empty $2p$ orbital via $p\pi-p\pi$ back-bonding.
   * Overlap efficiency depends on orbital size matching: $$2p_\pi(\text{B}) - 2p_\pi(\text{F}) > 2p_\pi(\text{B}) - 3p_\pi(\text{Cl}) > 2p_\pi(\text{B}) - 4p_\pi(\text{Br}) > 2p_\pi(\text{B}) - 5p_\pi(\text{I})$$
   * In $\text{BF}_3$, maximum back-bonding relieves the electron deficiency of Boron, making it the weakest Lewis acid. In $\text{BI}_3$, poor $2p-5p$ overlap results in negligible back-bonding, making it the strongest Lewis acid.
* Hydrolysis Behavior:
   * $\text{BCl}_3, \text{BBr}_3, \text{BI}_3$ undergo complete, irreversible hydrolysis: $$\text{BCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 + 3\text{HCl}$$
   * $\text{BF}_3$ hydrolyzes partially because released $\text{HF}$ coordinates with unreacted $\text{BF}_3$ to form fluoroboric acid: $$4\text{BF}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 + 3\text{H}[\text{BF}_4]$$

3. Group 14 Elements: The Carbon Family
3.1 Electronic Configuration & Physical Properties
* Valence shell configuration: $ns^2 np^2$.
* Elements: Carbon ($\text{C}$, non-metal), Silicon ($\text{Si}$, metalloid), Germanium ($\text{Ge}$, metalloid), Tin ($\text{Sn}$, metal), Lead ($\text{Pb}$, metal).
* Catenation Power:
   * Property of forming long covalent chains and rings. Decreases rapidly down the group as bond energy decreases: $$\mathbf{\text{C} \gg \text{Si} > \text{Ge} \approx \text{Sn} \quad (\text{Pb shows zero catenation})}$$ $$\text{C}-\text{C } (348\text{ kJ/mol}) > \text{Si}-\text{Si } (297\text{ kJ/mol}) > \text{Ge}-\text{Ge } (260\text{ kJ/mol}) > \text{Sn}-\text{Sn } (240\text{ kJ/mol})$$
* Oxidation States & Redox Behavior:
   * $+4$ and $+2$ oxidation states exist.
   * Inert pair effect stabilizes $+2$ for heavier elements:
      * $+2$ Stability: $\mathbf{\text{Ge}^{2+} < \text{Sn}^{2+} < \text{Pb}^{2+}}$.
      * $+4$ Stability: $\mathbf{\text{C}^{4+} > \text{Si}^{4+} > \text{Ge}^{4+} > \text{Sn}^{4+} > \text{Pb}^{4+}}$.
   * Consequences:
      * $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ is a reducing agent ($\text{Sn}^{2+} \to \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^-$).
      * $\text{Pb}^{4+}$ is a strong oxidizing agent ($\text{Pb}^{4+} + 2e^- \to \text{Pb}^{2+}$), meaning $\text{PbO}_2$ and $\text{PbCl}_4$ easily reduce to $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ salts. $\text{PbI}_4$ does not exist because $\text{I}^-$ reduces $\text{Pb}^{4+}$.

	4.2 Fullerene Topology Rules
* In $\text{C}_{60}$, there are 20 six-membered rings (hexagons) and 12 five-membered rings (pentagons).
* Euler's Polyhedral Invariant: A closed fullerene cage composed of pentagons and hexagons must contain exactly 12 pentagons, regardless of the total number of carbon atoms: $$N_{\text{pentagons}} = 12, \qquad N_{\text{hexagons}} = \frac{n - 20}{2} \quad (\text{for } \text{C}_n)$$
* Isolated Pentagon Rule (IPR): No two pentagons share an edge in stable fullerenes. Each pentagon is fused exclusively to five hexagons. Hexagons are fused to both hexagons and pentagons.

5. Oxides & Halides of Carbon and Silicon
5.1 Carbon Monoxide ($\text{CO}$)
* Preparation:
   * Dehydration of formic acid by concentrated sulphuric acid: $$\text{HCOOH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4, \Delta} \text{CO} \uparrow + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
   * Industrial producer gas: $2\text{C} + \text{O}_2 + 4\text{N}_2 \to 2\text{CO} + 4\text{N}_2$; Water gas (syngas): $\text{C} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{CO} + \text{H}_2$.
* Electronic Structure: $:C \equiv O:$ with a coordinate covalent bond from $\text{O}$ to $\text{C}$. Acts as a strong $\sigma$-donor and $\pi$-acceptor ligand, forming toxic carboxyhemoglobin (300 times more stable than oxyhemoglobin).
5.2 Carbon Dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) & Carbon Suboxide ($\text{C}_3\text{O}_2$)
* $\text{CO}_2$: Linear ($O=C=O$), non-polar ($\mu = 0$), weak acid forming carbonic acid $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ in water.
* Carbon Suboxide ($\text{C}_3\text{O}_2$):
   * Obtained by dehydrating malonic acid with phosphorus pentoxide: $$\text{CH}_2(\text{COOH})_2 \xrightarrow{\text{P}4\text{O}{10}, 150^\circ\text{C}} \text{O}=\text{C}=\text{C}=\text{C}=\text{O} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
   * Linear cumulative double-bond structure, toxic foul-smelling gas.
5.3 Silicon Tetrachloride ($\text{SiCl}_4$) vs. Carbon Tetrachloride ($\text{CCl}_4$)
* $\text{CCl}_4$ is completely inert to hydrolysis under ambient conditions because Carbon has no low-lying vacant $d$-orbitals to accept a lone pair from attacking $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules.
* $\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolyzes violently in water because Silicon can expand its coordination number by utilizing empty $3d$-orbitals: $$\text{SiCl}_4 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{Si}(\text{OH})_4 + 4\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{SiO}_2 \text{ (Silicic acid gel)}$$

6. Silicates & Silicones
![Silicates Classification And Silicones Polymerization](/media/silicates_classification_and_silicones_polymerization.webp) Description: Two-panel reference diagram: (Panel A) Comprehensive classification of silicates (ortho, pyro, cyclic, single chain, amphibole double chain, sheet, and 3D tektosilicates) detailing basic structural units, shared corner oxygens per tetrahedron, and mineral examples; (Panel B) Silicones industrial synthesis via Direct Process, controlled hydrolysis of chlorosilanes, chain termination, propagation, and cross-linking chemistry.
6.1 Classification of Silicates
All natural silicates are built from the fundamental tetrahedral structural unit $\mathbf{[\text{SiO}_4]^{4-}}$, where Silicon is $sp^3$ hybridized with a coordination number of 4.


1. Orthosilicates (Nesosilicates):
   * Structural unit: $[\text{SiO}_4]^{4-}$.
   * Shared oxygen vertices per tetrahedron: 0.
   * Examples: Phenacite ($\text{Be}_2\text{SiO}_4$), Willemite ($\text{Zn}_2\text{SiO}_4$), Forsterite ($\text{Mg}_2\text{SiO}_4$).
2. Pyrosilicates (Sorosilicates / Island Silicates):
   * Structural unit: $[\text{Si}_2\text{O}_7]^{6-}$.
   * Shared oxygen vertices: 1 corner oxygen atom shared between two tetrahedra.
   * Examples: Thortveitite ($\text{Sc}_2\text{Si}_2\text{O}_7$), Hemimorphite.
3. Cyclic / Ring Silicates:
   * General formula: $[(\text{SiO}_3)_n]^{2n-}$.
   * Shared oxygen vertices: 2 corners per tetrahedron.
   * Prominent examples:
      * Trimer ($n=3$): $[\text{Si}_3\text{O}_9]^{6-}$ in Wollastonite ($\text{Ca}_3\text{Si}_3\text{O}_9$).
      * Hexamer ($n=6$): $[\text{Si}6\text{O}{18}]^{12-}$ in Beryl ($\text{Be}_3\text{Al}_2\text{Si}6\text{O}{18}$).
4. Chain Silicates (Inosilicates):
   * Single Chain (Pyroxenes): Formula $[(\text{SiO}_3)_n]^{2n-}$, each tetrahedron shares 2 oxygen atoms with neighbors. Example: Diopside ($\text{CaMg}(\text{SiO}_3)_2$).
   * Double Chain (Amphiboles): Formula $[(\text{Si}4\text{O}{11})_n]^{6n-}$, tetrahedra alternately share 2 and 3 oxygen atoms (average $2.5$ shared corners). Example: Tremolite ($\text{Ca}_2\text{Mg}_5(\text{Si}4\text{O}{11})_2(\text{OH})_2$), Asbestos minerals.
5. Sheet Silicates (Phyllosilicates):
   * Structural unit: $[(\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5)_n]^{2n-}$.
   * Shared oxygen vertices: 3 corners per tetrahedron, forming a continuous 2D planar infinite network.
   * Examples: Talc ($\text{Mg}_3(\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5)_2(\text{OH})_2$, softest mineral), Kaolinite ($\text{Al}_2(\text{OH})_4(\text{Si}_2\text{O}_5)$), Mica.
6. Three-Dimensional / Framework Silicates (Tektosilicates):
   * Structural unit: $(\text{SiO}_2)_n$.
   * Shared oxygen vertices: All 4 corners shared with adjacent tetrahedra, forming a 3D covalent network.
   * Examples: Quartz, Tridymite, Cristobalite, Feldspars.
   * Zeolites: Microporous aluminosilicates where some $\text{Si}^{4+}$ ions in the 3D network are replaced by $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ions. The negative charge is balanced by exchangeable cations ($\text{Na}^+, \text{K}^+, \text{Ca}^{2+}$). Used as shape-selective catalysts (ZSM-5 converts alcohols directly into gasoline) and for softening hard water (Permutit process).
6.2 Silicones
Organosilicon polymers having general repeating units $\mathbf{[-R_2\text{Si}-\text{O}-]_n}$.


1. Synthesis Pathways:
   * Reaction of chloromethane with silicon in the presence of copper catalyst at $570\text{ K}$ (Direct Process): $$2\text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{Si} \xrightarrow{\text{Cu}, 570\text{ K}} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{SiCl}_2 \text{ (major)} + \text{CH}_3\text{SiCl}_3 + (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{SiCl} + \text{SiCl}_4$$
2. Controlled Polymerization:
   * Chain Propagator ($R_2\text{SiCl}_2$): Hydrolysis gives silanols that condense to form linear silicone polymers: $$(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{SiCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Si}(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{HCl}$$ $$n(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Si}(\text{OH})_2 \xrightarrow{-\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{---}\left[\text{Si}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{O}\right]_n\text{---}$$
   * Chain Stopper / Terminator ($R_3\text{SiCl}$): Monochlorosilane has only one hydrolyzable site, capping chain growth: $$2(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{SiCl} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{SiOH} \xrightarrow{-\text{H}_2\text{O}} (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{Si}-\text{O}-\text{Si}(\text{CH}_3)_3$$ (Used to regulate molecular weight and chain length).
   * Cross-Linking Agent ($R\text{SiCl}_3$): Trichlorosilane yields trihydroxy intermediates that cross-link adjacent chains into rigid 3D resins: $$\text{CH}_3\text{SiCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Si}(\text{OH})_3 + 3\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{-\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{Complex 3D Cross-linked Resins}$$
3. Properties & Applications:
   * Highly resistant to oxidation and thermal degradation due to strong $\text{Si}-\text{O}$ backbone bonds ($\sim 452\text{ kJ/mol}$).
   * Surrounded by non-polar organic alkyl groups, rendering them water-repellent (hydrophobic).
   * Excellent electrical insulators (high dielectric strength).
   * Viscosity remains almost constant over wide temperature ranges (used as lubricants in high-altitude aircraft).


________________


7. High-Yield JEE Traps & Exam Invariants
1. Gallium Expansion Trap:
   * Gallium expands by $3.1\%$ upon solidification. It should not be stored in glass or metal containers as it can break them upon freezing.
2. $\text{TlI}_3$ Formulation Trap:
   * $\text{TlI}_3$ is not a compound of $\text{Tl}^{3+}$. Due to the inert pair effect and the strong reducing power of iodide, it exists as an ionic compound containing thallous ion and triiodide ion: $$\mathbf{\text{TlI}_3 \equiv \text{Tl}^+ [\text{I}_3]^- = \text{Tl}^+ [\text{I}-\text{I}-\text{I}]^-}$$
3. Boric Acid Acidity Trap:
   * $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ does not dissociate as $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 \to \text{H}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{BO}_3^-$. It extracts $\text{OH}^-$ from water, acting as a monobasic Lewis acid, not a Brønsted acid.
4. Borax Hybridization Ratio:
   * In crystalline borax $[\text{B}_4\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4]^{2-}$, exactly two Boron atoms are $sp^2$ hybridized and two Boron atoms are $sp^3$ hybridized (ratio $1:1$).
5. Diborane Hydrogen Exchange Trap:
   * When $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$ is treated with excess deuterium gas ($\text{D}_2$), only the four terminal hydrogens exchange rapidly; the two bridging hydrogens exchange extremely slowly. Methylation of $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$ produces tetramethyldiborane $(\text{CH}_3)_4\text{B}_2\text{H}_2$—bridging hydrogens cannot be methylated without cleaving the dimer.
6. Carbon Monoxide Coordinate Bond Trap:
   * In $\text{CO}$, despite Oxygen being more electronegative than Carbon, the net dipole moment is very small ($0.11\text{ D}$) with the negative pole residing on Carbon, because the coordinate bond donates electron density from Oxygen to Carbon.
7. Lead Halides Stability Trap:
   * $\text{PbI}_4$ does not exist (instantaneous reduction: $\text{Pb}^{4+} + 2\text{I}^- \to \text{Pb}^{2+} + \text{I}_2$).
   * $\text{PbF}_4$ and $\text{PbCl}_4$ exist because fluorine and chlorine cannot reduce $\text{Pb}^{4+}$.

title: s-Block Elements: Alkali & Alkaline Earth Metals (Groups 1 & 2)
content:
Chemistry Revision Context: Chapter 77 — s-Block Elements: Alkali & Alkaline Earth Metals (Groups 1 & 2)
Source: Coaching Modules & Advanced Theory Sheets (scraped/Coaching_Modules/.../CLASS-11 (JA)/CHEMISTRY/s-Block Elements/, ADV_SBC_Th_E.pdf, ADV_SBC_Ex_B.pdf, ADV_SBC_Ex_E.pdf, ADV_SBC_APSP_E.pdf) Extracted into: JEE/context/ Batch: Inorganic Chemistry Core — Group 1 (Alkali Metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) Electronic Configuration $ns^1$, Flame Test Emission Spectra ($\text{Li}$ crimson red, $\text{Na}$ golden yellow, $\text{K}$ lilac, $\text{Rb}$ red-violet, $\text{Cs}$ sky blue), Density Inversion ($\text{K} < \text{Na}$), Hydration Enthalpy vs. Ionic Mobility Reversal in Aqueous Solutions ($\text{Li}^+ < \text{Na}^+ < \text{K}^+ < \text{Rb}^+ < \text{Cs}^+$), Standard Reduction Potentials ($E^\circ$ for $\text{Li}^+/\text{Li} = -3.04\text{ V}$, strongest reducing agent in water due to maximum hydration enthalpy), Solutions in Liquid Ammonia (Dilute paramagnetic deep blue with ammoniated electrons vs. Concentrated $>3\text{ M}$ bronze/copper diamagnetic with paired electrons); Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra) Electronic Configuration $ns^2$, Flame Test ($\text{Ca}$ brick red, $\text{Sr}$ crimson, $\text{Ba}$ apple green; $\text{Be}, \text{Mg}$ colorless due to high excitation energy), Ionization Enthalpy Parities ($\text{IE}_1(\text{Group 2}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{Group 1})$ but $\text{IE}_2(\text{Group 2}) \ll \text{IE}_2(\text{Group 1})$), Anomalous Properties of $\text{Li}$ and $\text{Be}$, Diagonal Relationships ($\text{Li}-\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Be}-\text{Al}$), Oxides, Peroxides, Superoxides ($\text{Li}_2\text{O}$ normal oxide, $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$ peroxide, $\text{KO}_2, \text{RbO}_2, \text{CsO}_2$ paramagnetic superoxides with 1 unpaired electron in $\pi^* 2p$), Industrial Manufacture ($\text{NaOH}$ via Castner-Kellner mercury cathode cell and Nelson diaphragm cell; Metallic $\text{Na}$ via Down's process using molten $\text{NaCl} + \text{CaCl}_2$; $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ Soda Ash via Solvay ammonia-soda process and why $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$ cannot be prepared by Solvay), Thermal Stability & Solubility Invariants (Carbonates $\text{BeCO}_3 < \dots < \text{BaCO}_3$; Hydroxides solubility increases down group; Sulphates solubility decreases $\text{BeSO}_4 > \dots > \text{BaSO}_4$; Nitrates thermal decomposition parity), Calcium Compounds & Industrial Building Materials (Quicklime $\text{CaO}$ lime kiln calcination, Slaked lime $\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$, Gypsum $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, Plaster of Paris $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$, Dead burnt plaster $\text{CaSO}_4$, Portland cement composition and setting), Carbides (Methanides, Acetylides, Allylides), and Comprehensive High-Yield JEE Traps. Status: Verified, LaTeX-Validated, and Formatted with Preserved Visual Diagrams


________________


1. Group 1: The Alkali Metals
![S Block Flame Test And Hydration Trends](/media/s_block_flame_test_and_hydration_trends.webp) Description: Two-panel reference diagram: (Panel A) Characteristic flame test emissions and visible wavelengths for alkali and alkaline earth metals; (Panel B) Crystalline ionic radius vs. hydrated radius and the resulting aqueous ionic mobility inversion ($\text{Li}^+ < \text{Na}^+ < \text{K}^+ < \text{Rb}^+ < \text{Cs}^+$).
1.1 Electronic Structure & Periodic Trends
* Outer Configuration: $ns^1$. Univalent cations ($\text{M}^+$) readily formed due to low first ionization enthalpy ($\text{IE}_1$).
* Physical Properties Matrix:

	1.2 Key Anomalies & Invariants in Group 1
1. Density Anomaly ($\text{K} < \text{Na}$):
   * Normal trend: Density increases down the group.
   * Anomaly: $\mathbf{\text{K} (0.86\text{ g/cm}^3) < \text{Na} (0.97\text{ g/cm}^3)}$.
   * Cause: The introduction of the $3d$ subshell in potassium causes an abnormal expansion in atomic volume that outweighs the increase in atomic mass.
2. Hydration Enthalpy vs. Ionic Mobility Inversion:
   * Degree of hydration depends inversely on ionic size: $$\mathbf{\text{Li}^+ > \text{Na}^+ > \text{K}^+ > \text{Rb}^+ > \text{Cs}^+} \quad (\text{Hydration Enthalpy & Hydrated Radius})$$
   * Because $\text{Li}^+$ carries a dense hydration sphere of water dipoles, its effective hydrated size is largest, dragging water molecules through solution.
   * Consequently, aqueous ionic mobility and electrical conductance are reversed: $$\mathbf{\text{Li}^+ < \text{Na}^+ < \text{K}^+ < \text{Rb}^+ < \text{Cs}^+} \quad (\text{Aqueous Conductance})$$
3. Reducing Power & Standard Electrode Potential ($E^\circ$):
   * Standard reduction potential $E^\circ$ is governed by the Born-Haber cycle for ionization and hydration: $$\text{M}(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\text{sub}} H} \text{M}(g) \xrightarrow{\Delta_i H} \text{M}^+(g) \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H} \text{M}^+(aq)$$
   * Although $\text{Li}$ has the highest ionization energy among alkali metals, its exceptionally large exothermic hydration enthalpy ($\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H^\circ = -506\text{ kJ/mol}$) overcompensates, giving it the most negative reduction potential ($E^\circ = -3.04\text{ V}$).
   * Reducing power in aqueous solution: $\mathbf{\text{Li} > \text{K} \approx \text{Rb} \approx \text{Cs} > \text{Na}}$.
   * Reducing power in gaseous state (vapor phase): $\mathbf{\text{Cs} > \text{Rb} > \text{K} > \text{Na} > \text{Li}}$ (governed strictly by $\text{IE}_1$).
1.3 Solutions of Alkali Metals in Liquid Ammonia
Alkali metals dissolve smoothly in liquid ammonia without hydrogen evolution to yield distinctive solutions depending on concentration:


1. Dilute Solutions ($<3\text{ M}$): $$\text{M} + (x + y)\text{NH}_3 \longrightarrow \underbrace{[\text{M}(\text{NH}_3)x]^+}{\text{Ammoniated Cation}} + \underbrace{[e(\text{NH}_3)y]^-}{\text{Ammoniated Electron}}$$
   * Color: Deep Blue (due to absorption of red photons by ammoniated electrons).
   * Magnetic Nature: Paramagnetic (due to single unpaired ammoniated electrons).
   * Electrical Conductivity: Excellent conductor (both ammoniated cations and ammoniated electrons act as charge carriers).
   * Chemical Character: Powerful reducing agent (Birch reduction converts alkynes to trans-alkenes).
2. Concentrated Solutions ($>3\text{ M}$):
   * Ammoniated electrons pair up: $2[e(\text{NH}_3)_y]^- \to [e_2(\text{NH}3){2y}]^{2-}$.
   * Color: Changes from deep blue to metallic bronze/copper.
   * Magnetic Nature: Diamagnetic (all spins paired).
   * Conductivity decreases toward metallic values.
3. Decomposition upon Standing or Catalysis: $$\text{M} + \text{NH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Fe catalyst / Impurities}} \text{MNH}_2 \text{ (Amide)} + \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2 \uparrow$$


________________


2. Group 2: The Alkaline Earth Metals
2.1 General Characteristics & Trends
* Valence configuration: $ns^2$. Divalent cations ($\text{M}^{2+}$) form readily.
* Ionization Enthalpies ($\text{IE}_1$ vs. $\text{IE}_2$):
   * $\text{IE}_1(\text{Group 2}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{Group 1})$ due to higher effective nuclear charge and smaller atomic size.
   * $\text{IE}_2(\text{Group 2}) \ll \text{IE}_2(\text{Group 1})$ because removing the second electron in Group 1 disrupts a noble gas core, whereas in Group 2 it achieves an inert gas configuration ($\text{M}^{2+}$).
   * In aqueous solution or solid lattice, the high hydration energy and lattice energy of $\text{M}^{2+}$ overcompensate for $\text{IE}_2$, ensuring that univalent $\text{M}^+$ compounds of Group 2 do not exist.
* Flame Colors:
   * Calcium ($\text{Ca}$): Brick Red ($622\text{ nm}$)
   * Strontium ($\text{Sr}$): Crimson Red ($606\text{ nm}$)
   * Barium ($\text{Ba}$): Apple Green ($524\text{ nm}$)
   * Radium ($\text{Ra}$): Crimson
   * $\text{Be}$ and $\text{Mg}$ do not impart color to the Bunsen flame because their valence electrons are tightly bound by the compact nucleus and cannot be excited by flame thermal energy.
2.2 Anomalous Behavior of Lithium and Beryllium & Diagonal Relationships
1. Lithium vs. Group 1:
   * $\text{Li}$ is much harder and has a higher melting/boiling point.
   * $\text{Li}$ reacts directly with nitrogen to form ionic nitride ($\text{Li}_3\text{N}$); other alkali metals do not form stable nitrides.
   * $\text{LiOH}$ is a weak base and decomposes on heating to $\text{Li}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$; other alkali hydroxides do not decompose.
   * $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$ is thermally unstable, decomposing to $\text{Li}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$; other alkali carbonates are thermally stable.
   * $\text{LiNO}_3$ decomposes on heating to $\text{Li}_2\text{O} + \text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$; other alkali nitrates decompose to nitrites $\text{MNO}_2 + \text{O}_2$.
   * $\text{LiF}$ and $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$ are sparingly soluble in water due to high lattice energy.
2. Diagonal Relationship: $\text{Li}$ and $\text{Mg}$:
   * Arises from similar ionic potential (charge-to-size ratio): $\phi(\text{Li}^+) \approx \phi(\text{Mg}^{2+})$ ($0.76\text{ \AA}$ vs. $0.72\text{ \AA}$).
   * Both form nitrides ($\text{Li}_3\text{N}$ and $\text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2$).
   * Both form normal oxides ($\text{Li}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{MgO}$) rather than peroxides or superoxides.
   * Both chlorides are deliquescent and crystallize as hydrates ($\text{LiCl}\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$); both are soluble in ethanol.
   * Both carbonates decompose on heating to release $\text{CO}_2$.
3. Diagonal Relationship: $\text{Be}$ and $\text{Al}$:
   * Both have similar charge-to-radius ratio ($\phi \approx 64/31 \approx 2.1$).
   * Both metals are rendered passive by concentrated nitric acid due to protective oxide films.
   * Both oxides and hydroxides are amphoteric: $$\text{Be}(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \longrightarrow [\text{Be}(\text{OH})_4]^{2-} \text{ (Beryllate)}$$ $$\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3 + \text{OH}^- \longrightarrow [\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]^- \text{ (Aluminate)}$$
   * Both chlorides ($\text{BeCl}_2$ and $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$) have bridged chloro structures in the vapor/solid phase and act as Lewis acids (catalysts in Friedel-Crafts reactions).
   * Both form carbide methanides ($\text{Be}_2\text{C}$ and $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$) which hydrolyze to give methane gas ($\text{CH}_4$).
   * Beryllium has a maximum coordination number of 4 due to absence of $d$-orbitals, forming $[\text{BeF}_4]^{2-}$.


________________


3. Oxides, Peroxides & Superoxides
3.1 Reaction of Alkali Metals with Oxygen
The nature of the primary oxide formed on burning alkali metals in excess air depends directly on the cation size: $$\mathbf{\text{Li} \longrightarrow \text{Li}_2\text{O} \text{ (Monoxide)}}, \qquad \mathbf{\text{Na} \longrightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 \text{ (Peroxide)}}, \qquad \mathbf{\text{K, Rb, Cs} \longrightarrow \text{MO}_2 \text{ (Superoxide)}}$$


* Lattice Energy Stability Rule:
   * Small cations ($\text{Li}^+$) stabilize small anions ($\text{O}^{2-}$ oxide) via high lattice energy.
   * Intermediate cations ($\text{Na}^+$) stabilize intermediate anions ($\text{O}_2^{2-}$ peroxide).
   * Large cations ($\text{K}^+, \text{Rb}^+, \text{Cs}^+$) stabilize large, polarizable polyatomic anions ($\text{O}_2^-$ superoxide) via lattice energy and low polarization.
* Hydrolysis Reactions Matrix:
   * Normal Oxide: $\text{M}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{M}^+ + 2\text{OH}^-$
   * Peroxide: $\text{M}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{M}^+ + 2\text{OH}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2$
   * Superoxide: $2\text{MO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{M}^+ + 2\text{OH}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{O}_2 \uparrow$
* Magnetic & Electronic Nature:
   * Peroxide ($\text{O}_2^{2-}$): Total 18 electrons; $\sigma^* 2p^2$ fully paired $\implies$ Diamagnetic, colorless.
   * Superoxide ($\text{O}_2^-$): Total 17 electrons; $\pi^* 2p^3$ has one unpaired electron $\implies$ Paramagnetic, colored (yellow/orange). $\text{KO}_2$ is used as an oxygen generator and $\text{CO}_2$ scrubber in submarines and spacecraft: $$4\text{KO}_2 + 2\text{CO}_2 \longrightarrow 2\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 + 3\text{O}_2 \uparrow$$ $$4\text{KO}_2 + 4\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 4\text{KHCO}_3 + 3\text{O}_2 \uparrow$$


________________


4. Industrial Manufacture of Sodium Compounds
![S Block Industrial Cells And Thermal Stability](/media/s_block_industrial_cells_and_thermal_stability.webp) Description: Two-panel industrial reference diagram: (Panel A) Technical layouts of Castner-Kellner cell, Down's electrolytic cell, and Solvay soda ash synthesis; (Panel B) Thermal stability rankings of carbonates and nitrates alongside solubility inversions of hydroxides, sulphates, and fluorides.
4.1 Sodium Hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$ / Caustic Soda)
Commercial manufacture is carried out via the electrolysis of brine ($\text{NaCl}$ solution):


1. Castner-Kellner Cell (Mercury Cathode Process):
   * Anode: Carbon/Graphite blocks.
   * Cathode: Flowing pool of mercury ($\text{Hg}$) at the bottom of the cell.
   * Electrochemical Reactions: $$\text{Anode: } 2\text{Cl}^- \longrightarrow \text{Cl}_2(g) \uparrow + 2e^-$$ $$\text{Cathode: } \text{Na}^+ + e^- + \text{Hg} \longrightarrow \text{Na/Hg (Sodium Amalgam)}$$
   * Denuder Tank: The sodium amalgam is transferred to a separate chamber and treated with water: $$2\text{Na/Hg} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + 2\text{Hg} \downarrow \text{ (recycled)} + \text{H}_2(g) \uparrow$$
   * Yields exceptionally pure $\text{NaOH}$ free from chloride contamination.
2. Reactions of $\text{NaOH}$ with Halogens:
   * With cold, dilute $\text{NaOH}$ (Disproportionation to halide and hypohalite): $$2\text{NaOH} + \text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Cold, dil.}} \text{NaCl} + \text{NaOCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
   * With hot, concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ (Disproportionation to halide and chlorate): $$6\text{NaOH} + 3\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Hot, conc.}} 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
3. Reaction with Amphoteric Metals: $$\text{Zn} + 2\text{NaOH} \longrightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{ZnO}_2 \text{ (Sodium zincate)} + \text{H}_2 \uparrow$$ $$2\text{Al} + 2\text{NaOH} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{NaAlO}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \uparrow$$ $$\text{Sn} + 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SnO}_3 \text{ (Sodium stannite)} + 2\text{H}_2 \uparrow$$
4.2 Sodium Carbonate ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$ / Washing Soda) & Solvay Process
1. Reaction Sequence of Solvay (Ammonia-Soda) Process:
   * Carbon dioxide is bubbled through brine saturated with ammonia: $$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \longrightarrow (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$$ $$(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \longrightarrow 2\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$$ $$\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3 + \text{NaCl} \longrightarrow \mathbf{\text{NaHCO}_3 \downarrow \text{ (precipitates)}} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$
   * Sodium hydrogen carbonate crystals are filtered and calcined: $$2\text{NaHCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \uparrow \text{ (recycled)}$$
   * Ammonia recovery: Ammonium chloride filtrate is boiled with milk of lime: $$2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2 \longrightarrow 2\text{NH}_3 \uparrow \text{ (recycled)} + \mathbf{\text{CaCl}_2 \text{ (only major byproduct)}}$$
2. Why Potassium Carbonate ($\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$) Cannot Be Prepared by Solvay Process:
   * Potassium hydrogen carbonate ($\text{KHCO}_3$) is fairly soluble in water and does not precipitate upon adding $\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$ to $\text{KCl}$ solution.
3. Efflorescence of Washing Soda: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{Dry air}} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (Monohydrate)} + 9\text{H}_2\text{O} \uparrow \xrightarrow{>373\text{ K}} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \text{ (Soda ash, anhydrous)}$$


________________


5. Important Compounds of Alkaline Earth Metals
![Lime Kiln Quicklime Calcination](/media/lime_kiln_quicklime_calcination.webp) Description: Industrial rotary lime kiln used for thermal calcination of calcium carbonate limestone to quicklime ($CaO$) at $1070-1270\text{ K}$.
5.1 Calcium Oxide ($\text{CaO}$ / Quicklime)
* Preparation: Thermal calcination of limestone in a rotary kiln at $1070-1270\text{ K}$: $$\text{CaCO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2 \uparrow \quad (\Delta H = +178\text{ kJ/mol})$$
   * Carbon dioxide is continuously vented to shift equilibrium forward.
* Properties:
   * Slaking of Lime (Highly Exothermic): $\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$ ($\Delta H = -65\text{ kJ/mol}$).
   * Quicklime slaked with caustic soda produces Soda Lime ($\text{NaOH} + \text{CaO}$).
   * Basic flux: $\text{CaO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{CaSiO}_3$ (slag in iron blast furnace).
5.2 Calcium Hydroxide ($\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$ / Slaked Lime)
* Clear aqueous solution is called Lime Water; a suspension of slaked lime in water is called Milk of Lime.
* Reaction with Chlorine Gas: $$2\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{Cl}_2 \longrightarrow \underbrace{\text{CaCl}_2 + \text{Ca}(\text{OCl})_2 + 2\text{H}2\text{O}}{\mathbf{\text{Bleaching Powder: } \text{Ca}(\text{OCl})_2 \cdot \text{CaCl}_2 \cdot \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}}}$$
5.3 Calcium Sulphate, Gypsum & Plaster of Paris
![Calcium Sulphate Gypsum Pop Cycle](/media/calcium_sulphate_gypsum_pop_cycle.webp) Description: Flowchart illustrating the thermal hydration-dehydration cycle between Gypsum ($CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O$), Plaster of Paris ($CaSO_4 \cdot 0.5H_2O$), and Dead Burnt Plaster ($CaSO_4$).


![Potassium Sulphate Reactions Chart](/media/potassium_sulphate_reactions_chart.webp) Description: Reaction pathways and synthetic derivatives of potassium sulphate ($K_2SO_4$) from schonite and kainite minerals.


![Magnesium Sulphate Epsom Chart](/media/magnesium_sulphate_epsom_chart.webp) Description: Synthesis and hydration equilibria of magnesium sulphate heptahydrate ($MgSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O$, Epsom salt) from kieserite, magnesite, and dolomite.


1. Hydration & Heating Cycle: $$\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (Gypsum)} \xrightarrow{393\text{ K } (120^\circ\text{C})} \mathbf{\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (Plaster of Paris)}} + \frac{3}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ $$\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{>393\text{ K}} \mathbf{\text{CaSO}_4 \text{ (Dead Burnt Plaster)}} \xrightarrow{>1373\text{ K}} \text{CaO} + \text{SO}_2 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$$
2. Setting of Plaster of Paris:
   * When mixed with water, POP forms a plastic mass that hardens in $10-15$ minutes with an expansion of $\sim 1\%$ in volume (enabling sharp casting of statues and surgical molds): $$\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{+\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (orthorhombic)} \xrightarrow{\text{Hardening}} \text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (monoclinic)}$$
   * Retarders: Glycerol, borax, glue retard setting. Accelerators: Alum, $\text{NaCl}$ accelerate setting.
   * Keene's Cement: POP mixed with alum and ignited sets into an extremely hard marble-like finish.
5.4 Portland Cement
* Raw Materials: Limestone ($\text{CaCO}_3$) providing $\text{CaO}$ ($50-60\%$) and Clay providing $\text{SiO}_2$ ($20-25\%$), $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ ($5-10\%$), $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ ($1-2\%$).
* Major Ingredients:
   * Dicalcium silicate ($\text{Ca}_2\text{SiO}_4$ or $\text{C}_2\text{S}$): $26\%$ (provides ultimate long-term strength).
   * Tricalcium silicate ($\text{Ca}_3\text{SiO}_5$ or $\text{C}_3\text{S}$): $51\%$ (rapid initial hydration and setting).
   * Tricalcium aluminate ($\text{Ca}_3\text{Al}_2\text{O}_6$ or $\text{C}_3\text{A}$): $11\%$ (fastest setting; initiates flash setting).
   * Tetracalcium aluminoferrite ($\text{Ca}_4\text{Al}_2\text{Fe}2\text{O}{10}$ or $\text{C}_4\text{AF}$): $9\%$.
* Role of Gypsum in Cement:
   * Raw cement clinker is mixed with $2-3\%$ Gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$) before fine grinding.
   * Function: Gypsum reacts with $\text{C}_3\text{A}$ to form insoluble calcium sulfoaluminate ($\text{C}_3\text{A} \cdot 3\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 32\text{H}_2\text{O}$), retarding the initial rapid hydration and preventing flash setting, allowing sufficient working time for mortar placement.


________________


6. Thermal Stability & Solubility Invariants
6.1 Thermal Stability Hierarchy of Polyatomic Salts
For salts containing large oxyanions ($\text{CO}_3^{2-}, \text{SO}_4^{2-}, \text{NO}_3^-$), thermal stability is controlled by the polarizing power (charge/radius ratio) of the cation (Fajan's rule):


* High polarizing power cations ($\text{Be}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Li}^+$) strongly distort the electron cloud of the oxyanion, pulling electron density into a covalent bond with oxygen and facilitating decomposition into a stable oxide and volatile gas ($\text{CO}_2, \text{SO}_3, \text{NO}_2$).
* Carbonates Stability: $$\mathbf{\text{BeCO}_3 < \text{MgCO}_3 < \text{CaCO}_3 < \text{SrCO}_3 < \text{BaCO}_3}$$ $$\text{BeCO}_3 \text{ decomposes below } 100^\circ\text{C (must be stored in } \text{CO}_2 \text{ atmosphere); } \text{BaCO}_3 \text{ stable up to } 1360^\circ\text{C.}$$
* Sulphates Stability: $$\mathbf{\text{BeSO}_4 < \text{MgSO}_4 < \text{CaSO}_4 < \text{SrSO}_4 < \text{BaSO}_4}$$
6.2 Solubility Trends in Water
Solubility in water depends on the competition between Lattice Energy ($U$) and Hydration Energy ($\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H$):


1. Hydroxides of Group 2: $$\mathbf{\text{Be}(\text{OH})_2 < \text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2 < \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2 < \text{Sr}(\text{OH})_2 < \text{Ba}(\text{OH})_2} \quad (\text{Solubility Increases Down Group})$$
   * Hydroxide ($\text{OH}^-$) is a small anion. As cation radius increases down the group, lattice energy decreases much faster than hydration energy ($U \propto \frac{1}{r_+ + r_-}$), making $\Delta H_{\text{solution}}$ more favorable.
2. Sulphates of Group 2: $$\mathbf{\text{BeSO}_4 > \text{MgSO}_4 > \text{CaSO}_4 > \text{SrSO}_4 > \text{BaSO}_4} \quad (\text{Solubility Decreases Down Group})$$
   * Sulphate ($\text{SO}4^{2-}$) is a large anion. The lattice energy remains almost constant down the group because $r-$ dominates ($r_+ + r_- \approx r_-$). Meanwhile, hydration energy of the cation drops precipitously ($\Delta_{\text{hyd}} H \propto \frac{1}{r_+}$). Thus, hydration enthalpy is insufficient to overcome lattice energy for $\text{BaSO}_4$.
3. Fluorides vs. Other Halides:
   * $\text{BeF}_2$ is highly soluble in water due to immense hydration energy of tiny $\text{Be}^{2+}$.
   * $\text{MgF}_2$ is the least soluble fluoride of the group due to high lattice energy.


________________


7. High-Yield JEE Traps & Exam Invariants
1. Nitrate Decomposition Duality:
   * Group 1 nitrates (except $\text{Li}$) decompose at $500^\circ\text{C}$ to nitrites without brown fumes: $$2\text{NaNO}_3 \xrightarrow{500^\circ\text{C}} 2\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \uparrow$$
   * $\text{LiNO}_3$ and all Group 2 nitrates decompose to oxides, liberating brown $\text{NO}_2$ fumes: $$4\text{LiNO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{Li}_2\text{O} + 4\text{NO}_2 \uparrow + \text{O}_2 \uparrow$$ $$2\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_2 \uparrow + \text{O}_2 \uparrow$$
2. Carbide Hydrolysis Classification:
   * Methanides ($C^{4-}$): $\text{Be}_2\text{C} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Be}(\text{OH})_2 + \text{CH}_4 \uparrow$; $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{Al}(\text{OH})_3 + 3\text{CH}_4 \uparrow$.
   * Acetylides ($C_2^{2-}$): $\text{CaC}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2 + \text{C}_2\text{H}_2 \uparrow$ (Ethyne).
   * Allylides ($C_3^{4-}$): $\text{Mg}_2\text{C}_3 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{Mg}(\text{OH})_2 + \text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH} \uparrow$ (Propyne).
3. Potassium Carbonate Solvay Impossibility:
   * $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$ cannot be synthesized via Solvay process because intermediate $\text{KHCO}_3$ is too soluble in water to precipitate out upon adding $\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$.
4. Alkali Metal Halides Hydration:
   * Only lithium halides form hydrates ($\text{LiCl}\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$); other alkali metal halides ($\text{NaCl}, \text{KCl}$) crystallize anhydrously from aqueous solution.
5. $\text{BeCl}_2$ Phase Polymorphism:
   * Solid state: Polymeric infinite chain with coordinate bonds; $\text{Be}$ is $sp^3$ hybridized with coordination number 4.
   * Vapor state ($<1200\text{ K}$): Chloro-bridged dimer $\text{Be}_2\text{Cl}_4$; $\text{Be}$ is $sp^2$ hybridized with coordination number 3.
   * High temperature vapor ($>1200\text{ K}$): Linear monomer $\text{Cl}-\text{Be}-\text{Cl}$; $\text{Be}$ is $sp$ hybridized with coordination number 2.

Chemistry Revision Context: Chapter 77 — s-Block Elements: Alkali & Alkaline Earth Metals (Groups 1 & 2)
Source: Coaching Modules & Advanced Theory Sheets (scraped/Coaching_Modules/.../CLASS-11 (JA)/CHEMISTRY/s-Block Elements/, ADV_SBC_Th_E.pdf, ADV_SBC_Ex_B.pdf, ADV_SBC_Ex_E.pdf, ADV_SBC_APSP_E.pdf) Extracted into: JEE/context/ Batch: Inorganic Chemistry Core — Group 1 (Alkali Metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) Electronic Configuration $ns^1$, Flame Test Emission Spectra ($\text{Li}$ crimson red, $\text{Na}$ golden yellow, $\text{K}$ lilac, $\text{Rb}$ red-violet, $\text{Cs}$ sky blue), Density Inversion ($\text{K} < \text{Na}$), Hydration Enthalpy vs. Ionic Mobility Reversal in Aqueous Solutions ($\text{Li}^+ < \text{Na}^+ < \text{K}^+ < \text{Rb}^+ < \text{Cs}^+$), Standard Reduction Potentials ($E^\circ$ for $\text{Li}^+/\text{Li} = -3.04\text{ V}$, strongest reducing agent in water due to maximum hydration enthalpy), Solutions in Liquid Ammonia (Dilute paramagnetic deep blue with ammoniated electrons vs. Concentrated $>3\text{ M}$ bronze/copper diamagnetic with paired electrons); Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra) Electronic Configuration $ns^2$, Flame Test ($\text{Ca}$ brick red, $\text{Sr}$ crimson, $\text{Ba}$ apple green; $\text{Be}, \text{Mg}$ colorless due to high excitation energy), Ionization Enthalpy Parities ($\text{IE}_1(\text{Group 2}) > \text{IE}_1(\text{Group 1})$ but $\text{IE}_2(\text{Group 2}) \ll \text{IE}_2(\text{Group 1})$), Anomalous Properties of $\text{Li}$ and $\text{Be}$, Diagonal Relationships ($\text{Li}-\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Be}-\text{Al}$), Oxides, Peroxides, Superoxides ($\text{Li}_2\text{O}$ normal oxide, $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$ peroxide, $\text{KO}_2, \text{RbO}_2, \text{CsO}_2$ paramagnetic superoxides with 1 unpaired electron in $\pi^* 2p$), Industrial Manufacture ($\text{NaOH}$ via Castner-Kellner mercury cathode cell and Nelson diaphragm cell; Metallic $\text{Na}$ via Down's process using molten $\text{NaCl} + \text{CaCl}_2$; $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ Soda Ash via Solvay ammonia-soda process and why $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$ cannot be prepared by Solvay), Thermal Stability & Solubility Invariants (Carbonates $\text{BeCO}_3 < \dots < \text{BaCO}_3$; Hydroxides solubility increases down group; Sulphates solubility decreases $\text{BeSO}_4 > \dots > \text{BaSO}_4$; Nitrates thermal decomposition parity), Calcium Compounds & Industrial Building Materials (Quicklime $\text{CaO}$ lime kiln calcination, Slaked lime $\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$, Gypsum $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, Plaster of Paris $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$, Dead burnt plaster $\text{CaSO}_4$, Portland cement composition and setting), Carbides (Methanides, Acetylides, Allylides), and Comprehensive High-Yield JEE Traps. Status: Verified, LaTeX-Validated, and Formatted with Preserved Visual Diagrams

1. Group 1: The Alkali Metals
![S Block Flame Test And Hydration Trends](/media/s_block_flame_test_and_hydration_trends.webp) Description: Two-panel reference diagram: (Panel A) Characteristic flame test emissions and visible wavelengths for alkali and alkaline earth metals; (Panel B) Crystalline ionic radius vs. hydrated radius and the resulting aqueous ionic mobility inversion ($\text{Li}^+ < \text{Na}^+ < \text{K}^+ < \text{Rb}^+ < \text{Cs}^+$).
1.1 Electronic Structure & Periodic Trends
* Outer Configuration: $ns^1$. Univalent cations ($\text{M}^+$) readily formed due to low first ionization enthalpy ($\text{IE}_1$).
* Physical Properties Matrix:
